title: Fvqkd: A Formal Verification Of Quantum Key Distribution Security In Rocq
authors: Ruixuan Deng, Zhengfeng Ji, Jiayu Zhang, Li Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD), whose security is derived from quantum mechanics rather than computational assumptions, is moving into standardization and commercial deployment. Yet its security guarantees rest on technically delicate proofs checked by hand. Formal verification closes this gap, establishing a two-factor assurance: unconditional security from physical principles, and machine-checked proofs against reasoning errors. We present FVQKD, a Rocq library for machine-checking QKD security proofs. Its first result is a complete, end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable, finite-key security for BB84. The mechanization reconstructs the complete proof infrastructure from first principles, including the smooth entropy framework, the entropic uncertainty relation, and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. It uncovers necessary side conditions that the published argument leaves unstated, one of which reveals a missing proof branch, and it grounds the information-theoretic bound in a formal semantics of protocol execution, which the pen-and-paper analysis lacks. The proof is entirely admit-free, relying only on the Rocq kernel and standard foundational axioms. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end formal verification of a QKD security proof. Built on MathComp, MathComp-Analysis, and CoqQ, the development provides quantum-information infrastructure designed for reuse across broader QKD variants and quantum cryptography applications.
tldr: FVQKD presents the first end-to-end machine-checked proof of composable finite-key security for BB84 in the Rocq proof assistant.
motivation: QKD security proofs are delicate and hand-checked, so formal verification can provide machine-checked assurance against reasoning errors while preserving unconditional security guarantees.
method: The authors build a Rocq library reconstructing smooth entropy, entropic uncertainty relations, the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma, and a formal semantics of protocol execution, then mechanize the BB84 finite-key composable security proof admit-free.
result: They obtain a complete admit-free machine-checked BB84 security proof, uncover unstated side conditions and a missing proof branch in the published argument, and provide reusable quantum-information infrastructure.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that QKD security proofs can be formally verified end-to-end and offers a foundation for machine-checking broader quantum cryptography protocols.

title: Probing Quasiperiodic Spectral Accessibility With A Finite-rate Quantum Otto Cycle
authors: Shujie Cheng, Lucas C. C\'eleri, Norton G. de Almeida, Gao Xianlong, G. D. de Moraes Neto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quasiperiodic systems combine sharply different spectral and localisation regimes with a dense hierarchy of dynamical time scales. We show that a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle can use this structure as a thermodynamic probe, revealing which parts of the spectrum become dynamically accessible and thermodynamically relevant during a driven transformation. For a generalised Aubry-Andr\'e-Harper chain, the resulting response is not determined by the static quasiperiodic regime alone: extended, near-critical, and crossing protocols do not exhibit universal ordering of work fluctuations. Instead, the statistics reflect transition pathways that are simultaneously dynamically coupled, thermally occupied, and energetically significant. The same spectral accessibility separates thermodynamic recovery from microscopic adiabatic recovery. Positive mean work can reappear while the population transfer dynamics remain strongly nonadiabatic because finite-rate population transfer is redistributed toward energetically less costly channels rather than suppressed. The full work distribution reveals a further separation, with a finite rate window in which positive-work cycles form a majority although the mean work remains negative. This behaviour persists in finite-size analysis. A thermally weighted spectral susceptibility connects these effects to a distributed hierarchy of dynamically active spectral regions rather than to a single minimum-gap bottleneck. Finite thermal contacts preserve this picture while introducing a second time scale and intercycle memory. Quantum Otto cycles can therefore provide a fluctuation-resolved thermodynamic probe of quasiperiodic spectral accessibility, complementary to direct spectroscopic and eigenstate-resolved diagnostics.
tldr: The paper shows that a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle can act as a thermodynamic probe of which spectral regions of a quasiperiodic Aubry-André-Harper chain become dynamically accessible and thermodynamically relevant.
motivation: Quasiperiodic systems have complex spectra and multiple dynamical timescales, making it unclear which spectral features actually control finite-time thermodynamic behavior. The authors aim to connect spectral accessibility to work fluctuations and nonadiabatic population transfer in a driven quantum heat-engine protocol.
method: They analyze a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle on a generalized Aubry-André-Harper chain, computing work distributions and population-transfer dynamics for extended, near-critical, and crossing protocols, including finite thermal contacts and finite-size effects.
result: They find no universal ordering of work fluctuations across static quasiperiodic regimes; instead, the statistics depend on transition pathways that are dynamically coupled, thermally occupied, and energetically significant. Positive mean work can reappear despite strong nonadiabaticity, and a finite rate window can yield a majority of positive-work cycles even when the mean work is negative.
conclusion: Finite-rate quantum Otto cycles provide a fluctuation-resolved thermodynamic probe of spectral accessibility in quasiperiodic systems, complementary to spectroscopic and eigenstate-resolved diagnostics, with thermal contacts adding a second timescale and intercycle memory.

Finite thermal contacts preserve this picture while introducing a second time scale and intercycle memory. deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a quantum Otto cycle consisting of two unitary driving strokes and two thermalization strokes with finite-time thermal contacts. The working medium is a generalized Aubry-André-Harper chain, which allows tuning between extended, critical, and localized regimes via a deformation parameter. The cycle is analyzed at finite rates, meaning the driving strokes are not perfectly adiabatic, and the work statistics are computed using the full counting statistics of work via the two-point measurement scheme. The dynamics during the driving strokes are simulated by solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (or master equation for open systems) for the many-body chain, and the work distribution is obtained from the joint probability distribution of energy measurements before and after each stroke. The authors also introduce a thermally weighted spectral susceptibility, defined as a sum over transitions weighted by thermal occupation and energy differences, to quantify the contribution of different spectral regions to the work fluctuations. Finite-size scaling is performed to check the robustness of the results, and the role of finite thermal contacts is examined by incorporating a second time scale and intercycle memory effects, likely through a collision model or a master equation with finite coupling.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that the work statistics of the Otto cycle are not determined solely by the static quasiperiodic regime. For extended, near-critical, and crossing protocols, the ordering of work fluctuations is not universal; instead, the statistics reflect the interplay of dynamical coupling, thermal occupation, and energetic significance of transitions. The authors find that positive mean work can reappear at finite rates even when the population transfer remains strongly nonadiabatic, because the finite-rate transfer is redistributed toward energetically less costly channels rather than being suppressed. Finite thermal contacts preserve this picture but introduce a second time scale and intercycle memory effects, which can modify the work statistics but do not qualitatively change the main conclusions.

title: All-photonic Millimeter-wave And Terahertz Signal Core At Room And Cryogenic Temperatures
authors: Jiawen Liu, Chengli Wang, Aleksei Gaier, Tianyi Zhang, Gabriel J\"ulg, Yazan Lampert, Andr\'e Garcia Primo, Alessandro Tomasino, Hua Li, Xin Ou, Ileana-Cristina Benea-Chelmus
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Millimeter-wave and terahertz technologies offer new opportunities for high-capacity communications, sensing, and quantum systems, but electronic signal chains above 100 GHz are limited by weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects. Photonic approaches mitigate these constraints by enabling chip-scale high-frequency components, yet existing implementations generally retain lossy off-chip electrical or free-space links, hindering dense and compact integration for cryogenic or space-constrained settings. Here, we show a monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip, termed a signal core, which generates, modulates, routes, and detects continuous-wave signals at discrete frequencies between 100 GHz and 2.5 THz. The architecture integrates high-frequency functional modules on chip and uses exclusively fiber-based optical interfaces. Bidirectional coherent electro-optic conversion enables signal generation, detection, and nanosecond-scale amplitude and phase modulation, while micro-coplanar striplines interconnect the modules into an end-to-end signal chain on a single chip. Our modules achieve single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g_0/2\pi=10 kHz and peak drive-power-normalized photon-flux conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection. It also operates at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator through the same fiber-only optical links. Together, these capabilities establish an all-photonic platform for millimeter-wave-to-terahertz systems and offer a broadly applicable architecture for applications constrained by electrical-interconnect loss, heat load, and footprint.
tldr: A monolithic lithium tantalate photonic chip generates, modulates, routes, and detects millimeter-wave/terahertz signals via all-optical fiber interfaces, including operation at 4 K.
motivation: High-frequency electronic signal chains above 100 GHz suffer from weak sources, noisy receivers, and lossy interconnects, motivating photonic alternatives for compact cryogenic and quantum-compatible systems.
method: The authors fabricate an integrated lithium tantalate electro-optic signal core with micro-coplanar striplines and fiber-only optical interfaces, enabling bidirectional coherent conversion and nanosecond modulation between optical and mm-wave/THz fields.
result: The chip operates from 100 GHz to 2.5 THz, achieves single-photon electro-optic coupling rates of g0/2π = 10 kHz and conversion efficiencies of 1.0%/mW for generation and 0.5%/mW for detection, and functions at 4 K in a dilution refrigerator.
conclusion: This all-photonic platform provides a scalable architecture for mm-wave-to-THz systems and is relevant to cryogenic quantum transduction where electrical-interconnect loss and heat load are limiting.

title: High-fidelity And Robust controlled-Z Gates For Superconducting Transmon Qubits. Ii. System-parameter Uncertainties And Overall Errors
authors: Hsi-Sheng Goan Chia-Hsien Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to [MATH] and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to [MATH] MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below [MATH]. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to [MATH] MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.
tldr: This paper develops optimal-control-designed controlled-Z gates for coupled tunable transmons that are robust against coupling, anharmonicity, and flux-frequency uncertainties.
motivation: High-fidelity two-qubit gates in superconducting processors suffer from intrinsic errors, decoherence, and device-parameter uncertainties that require frequent recalibration and limit scalability.
method: The authors extend an optimal-control framework to classify parameter uncertainties as off-diagonal coupling errors or diagonal detuning errors, suppress coupling errors via strong detuning modulation and dynamical decoupling, and optimize controls near a symmetric-detuning operating point under combined realistic error sources.
result: A 30-ns gate tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to the MHz range while keeping infidelity low, and a 24-ns gate near the symmetric-detuning point tolerates individual diagonal-parameter uncertainties at similar levels; stage-specific controls improve fidelity and robustness across six hardware-performance stages.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical route to fast, high-fidelity, robust CZ gates for superconducting transmon processors while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper (Part II of a two-part study) extends an optimal-control framework for designing high-fidelity controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons, previously developed in Part I to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors, by now incorporating parameter uncertainties. The authors classify uncertainties into two categories: those perturbing off-diagonal coupling strengths (coupling-strength errors) and those perturbing diagonal detunings (anharmonicities and zero-flux qubit frequencies). They identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated via dynamical decoupling generated by strong detuning modulation; for a 30-ns gate this reduces coupling error to 6.21×10⁻⁷ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to 2π×4 MHz while keeping total infidelity below 10⁻³. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances two dominant leakage-mediated interactions; a 24-ns gate near this point tolerates individual uncertainties up to 2π×5 MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. The authors then optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist, across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance, yielding stage-specific controls with lower infidelity and greater robustness. The work is positioned as a practical route to balancing speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead in large-scale superconducting processors.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The approach builds on the optimal-control framework of the companion paper (Part I), which designs CZ gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons while suppressing intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors. Here the control problem is augmented to include parameter uncertainties, which are partitioned by their effect on the Hamiltonian: off-diagonal coupling-strength perturbations versus diagonal detuning perturbations (anharmonicities and zero-flux frequencies). Rather than treating all uncertainties uniformly, the authors exploit the structure of each error class to design targeted suppression. For coupling errors, they rely on strong modulation of the detuning to induce an effective dynamical-decoupling behavior that averages out coupling-strength fluctuations. For detuning errors, they analyze the leakage-mediated interactions and locate a symmetric-detuning operating point where the two dominant contributions balance, minimizing sensitivity. The optimization is then repeated under realistic composite conditions—intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties together—across six staged hardware-performance scenarios, producing stage-specific pulse controls. The methodology is thus a structured, physics-informed robust-control design rather than a generic worst-case optimization, which is a notable methodological choice.
deep_read.results_analysis: The headline quantitative results are: for a 30-ns gate, coupling error is suppressed to 6.21×10⁻⁷, with tolerance to coupling-strength uncertainties up to 2π×4 MHz while total gate infidelity remains below 10⁻³. These numbers indicate that the robust-control design preserves fast gate times (24–30 ns) while maintaining error budgets compatible with fault-tolerant-relevant thresholds, though the 10⁻³ threshold itself is above the commonly cited ~10⁻⁴ surface-code target, so the reported tolerances should be read as robustness margins at a moderate fidelity level rather than at fault-tolerance-grade fidelities. The paper does not, in the provided text, give explicit infidelity values for the staged results, so the magnitude of improvement is asserted rather than quantified here.

title: Foresight-dependent Entropy Production In Stochastic Two-agent Dynamics

title: Pure States Are Optimal For Total Energy-constrained Quantum Channel Discrimination

abstract: ArXiv:2610.30295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the discrimination of two quantum channels acting on bosonic modes, with a probe state of fixed mean photon number and no ancilla. title: Dealing With Low-weight Errors That Lead Bp Osd To Fail
authors: Giacomo Fregona, Matthias C. L\"obl, Benjamin J. Brown, Michael J. Kastoryano, Stefano Paesani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Belief Propagation combined with Ordered Statistics Decoding (BP OSD) is an open-source decoding tool used widely within the community due to its versatility and ease of application to Quantum Low Density Parity Check (QLDPC) codes. However, the degeneracy of quantum codes has been observed to degrade the performance of BP OSD, particularly leading to error floors for low physical error rates. Here, we investigate the low-weight error configurations responsible for such failures in Bivariate Bicycle codes. We show that, at code capacity, BP OSD fails on errors whose weight is significantly smaller than d/2, arising from global symmetries of the decoding graph that prevent the convergence of parallel BP. Furthermore, our analysis reveals new pitfalls that can arise when analysing the performance of BP OSD in the rare events regime, such as loss of ergodicity in splitting methods and numerical instabilities in the decoder. We show how to mitigate these failure mechanisms by modifying the BP update rules and the decoder implementation, leading to substantial improvement in logical error rate.

title: Memory--Transport Competition In Physical Two-Bath Quantum Reset Dynamics
authors: Jishad Kumar, Achilleas Lazarides, Tapio Ala-Nissila
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherence preservation and environmental renewal offer competing ways of controlling quantum memory and transport. We show that a seemingly natural protocol which exactly replaces the bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system--bath coherences need not correspond to a physical fermionic state. We instead construct a two-reservoir protocol with independent, number-conserving thermal attenuators, for which complete positivity and fermionic admissibility hold by construction. Physical attenuation necessarily modifies bath populations as well as cross correlations; the coherence control is not an independent hard-reset knob. Quadratic dynamics reduces the stroboscopic problem to an exact matrix fixed-point equation without a weak-coupling or Markov approximation. Analytically, coherence retention enhances the leading short-cycle transfer rate, including the complete-erasure limit; no general endpoint-vanishing theorem exists. An exact stationary continuity theorem forces the through-current to vanish whenever either reservoir is left entirely unrefreshed, although no analogous theorem suppresses it at complete erasure. For biased structured reservoirs, exact finite-chain calculations display distinct coherence-, current-, and signed energy-transfer operating points; a resolved high-retention boundary layer exposes strong finite-size sensitivity of the coherence peak. The model provides a microscopic, fermion-admissible benchmark for the interplay of reservoir coherence, particle transport, and energetic exchange.

title: Mode-Selective Micromotion Compensation Via Coherent Excitation Of A Ground-State-Cooled Motional Mode
authors: Tetsu Kinase, Ippei Nakamura, Atsushi Noguchi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Excess micromotion induced by stray DC electric fields limits the control fidelity of trapped-ion experiments. Various techniques have been developed to detect and compensate ion displacements from the RF null by monitoring modulated fluorescence, ion positions, or micromotion sidebands. Although these approaches are effective, they do not probe the displacement through a ground-state-cooled motional mode and therefore offer limited compatibility with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols. Here, we demonstrate a micromotion compensation method based on the driven coherent amplitude of a ground-state-cooled motional mode. In this approach, the ion displacement is converted into a coherent motional excitation by an auxiliary RF drive and detected through the qubit. We determine the optimal compensation field with a [MATH] statistical uncertainty of 8 mV/m. The method is naturally compatible with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols employing nonclassical motional states, including Fock, squeezed, and Schr\"odinger-cat states, providing a pathway toward quantum-enhanced micromotion compensation.

title: Coherence And Imaginarity Of Qubit States Under Vanishing Bargmann Invariants
authors: Lin Chen Hao-Fan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Set coherence and set imaginarity are two important quantum resources defined by sets of states. We investigate tuples of qubit states under vanishing higher-order Bargmann invariants and show that their set coherence and set imaginarity are each related to whether they contain a pair of orthogonal states. Specifically, when the relevant higher-order Bargmann invariants vanish, the tuple contains a pair of orthogonal states if and only if removing some state makes the remaining tuple incoherent. Moreover, when maximally mixed states are excluded, the same vanishing conditions imply that the tuple is imaginarity-free if and only if it contains a pair of orthogonal states. As a consequence, under these conditions, a tuple of single-qubit states has imaginarity precisely when every tuple obtained by deleting one of its states is coherent.

result: Under the vanishing conditions, a tuple contains an orthogonal pair iff deleting some state makes the remainder incoherent; excluding maximally mixed states, imaginarity-freeness is equivalent to containing an orthogonal pair, so a tuple has imaginarity precisely when every one-state-deleted subtuple is coherent.

title: Distributed Dual-comb Spectroscopy
authors: Haowei Shi, Kartikeya Arora, Zheshen Zhang, Quntao Zhuang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose distributed dual-comb spectroscopy, a quantum-enhanced sensing architecture that simultaneously exploits spatial- and spectral-domain entanglement to improve the extraction of global spectroscopic information across broadband frequency ranges. These results establish a scalable route toward broadband distributed quantum spectroscopy with simultaneous spatial and spectral advantage.

title: Hierarchical Reduction Of Invariant Subspaces: From Fragmentation To Many-Body Scars

abstract: ArXiv:2610.30597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a hierarchy of invariant Hilbert-space structures connecting Hilbert-space fragmentation, partial solvability, and quantum many-body scars. Through the intermediate embedded space, local dynamics couples states from distinct frozen irreducible-string sectors and selects a new decomposition into representations, from which smaller invariant spaces can be retained. We also establish a rigidity constraint on isolating nonsymmetric towers and a constructive correspondence that transfers a reduction between locally realizable representations of the embedded dynamics. title: Normal-Form Characterization Of Adaptivity And Entanglement In Pauli-Based Computation
authors: Filipa C. R. Peres, Selman Ipek, Daniel Lovsted, Joshua Nevin, Anne Broadbent
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pauli-based computation (PBC) is a measurement-based model of quantum computation that samples from output distributions of universal Clifford+[MATH] circuits. Here, we provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes its adaptive and entanglement structures. These insights unify PBC with one-way quantum computing as dual or `time-reversed' counterparts. We use the NF to advance strategies for distributed computation and investigate magic-state injection rates. We also demonstrate an exponential improvement in the detection of unnecessary magic-state qubits, allowing their efficient removal. Our NF further enables ahead-of-time circuit compilation using PBC, reducing CNOT gate count and quantum memory of random quantum circuits on average by 50% and 40%, respectively, beating other state-of-the-art compilers.
tldr: The paper introduces a normal form for Pauli-based computation that fully characterizes its adaptivity and entanglement structures and uses it to improve distributed computation, magic-state handling, and circuit compilation.

result: The normal form enables an exponential improvement in detecting unnecessary magic-state qubits and achieves average reductions of about 50% in CNOT count and 40% in quantum memory for random circuits, outperforming state-of-the-art compilers.
conclusion: The work unifies Pauli-based computation with one-way quantum computing and provides a useful structural tool for distributed quantum computation and compiler optimization.

title: Exceptional Point Structure And Chiral State Transfer In A Rate-operator-engineered $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Bose-Hubbard Dimer
authors: Jaakko Luomala, Federico Settimo, Kimmo Luoma, Iiro Vilja, Jyrki Piilo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rate operator quantum jumps (ROQJ) is a general method to unravel a master equation describing the dynamics of an open quantum system into stochastic pure state trajectories. By post-selecting on no jumps occurring, one obtains a trajectory generated by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. The ROQJ allows for versatile modification of this non-Hermitian evolution, with each non-Hermitian Hamiltonian corresponding to a different continuous measurement scheme. We apply the ROQJ to modify the non-Hermitian dynamics of the open three-particle Bose-Hubbard dimer model under environmental non-local dephasing to construct a [MATH]-symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonians with a general two parameter [MATH]-symmetric imaginary diagonal part, which generalizes the well-known gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. We characterize the symmetry structure of the spectrum for different on-site interaction strengths. For vanishing on-site interaction, we find the unbroken [MATH]-symmetry region enclosed by order two exceptional lines of different character and four order four exceptional points, two of which are not found in the usual gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. Additionally, we find regions with degenerate imaginary parts of the eigenvalues, also not found in the gain-loss Bose-Hubbard dimer. In this parameter space, we use time-dependent rate operator transformations to investigate state transfer under slowly varying parameter loops. Loops encircling an order four exceptional point exhibit chiral state transfer. Because the loops cross exceptional lines, the final states are superpositions of eigenstates. Chiral state transfer is also found with non-zero homogeneous on-site interaction when the loop crosses over broken [MATH]-symmetry regions of different character. Using inhomogeneous on-site interactions, we find direction dependent state transfer between eigenstates without crossing or encircling exceptional points.

result: They find unbroken PT-symmetry regions bounded by second-order exceptional lines, four fourth-order exceptional points, and chiral state transfer for loops encircling exceptional points or crossing broken-symmetry regions; inhomogeneous interactions yield direction-dependent transfer without exceptional points.
conclusion: Rate-operator quantum jumps provide a versatile route to engineer non-Hermitian open-system dynamics and control state transfer through exceptional-point geometry.

title: Demand-Driven Routing Space For Lattice-Surgery Compilation
authors: Hanyu Wang, Wan-Hsuan Lin, Zihan Chen, Eddy Z. Zhang, Jason Cong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice-surgery compilation places logical qubits on a grid of surface-code tiles and routes their interactions. Sparse static layouts limit routing contention but reserve space that often remains idle. Reducing this reservation requires balancing area savings against additional gate serialization and qubit movement. In this paper, we present a co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space according to circuit demand. The architecture preserves a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while allowing its physical spacing to change between execution stages. The compiler coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to implement lattice surgeries using fewer physical qubits. Across our application benchmarks, our method reduces space-time volume by 55.6% in geometric mean and compiles 75.5 times faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration. A circuit-synthesis case study shows how our compiler exposes optimization tradeoffs.
tldr: A co-designed dynamic architecture and compiler that allocates routing space on demand for lattice-surgery-based surface-code compilation, cutting space-time volume substantially.
motivation: Static sparse layouts for lattice surgery avoid routing contention but reserve large idle areas; reducing this reservation naively causes gate serialization and extra qubit movement, so a demand-driven tradeoff is needed.
method: The authors keep a fixed virtual qubit floorplan while letting physical spacing vary between execution stages, and build a compiler that jointly coordinates placement, scheduling, and routing to realize lattice surgeries with fewer physical qubits.
result: Across application benchmarks, space-time volume drops by 55.6% in geometric mean and compilation is 75.5x faster than the evaluated DasCot configuration, with a circuit-synthesis case study illustrating the optimization tradeoffs.
conclusion: Demand-driven routing-space allocation offers a practical architecture-compiler co-design path to cheaper, faster fault-tolerant compilation, though the contribution is largely engineering-oriented EDA work.

title: On The Structure Of Quantum Finite-Level Systems: Decoherence-Free Subsystems, Quantum Nondemolition Variables, And Back-Action-Evading Measurements
authors: Jia Gu, Guofeng Zhang, Ian R. Petersen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The purpose of this paper is to conduct a comprehensive structural analysis of quantum finite-level systems in the Heisenberg picture, where the evolution of system observables is modeled by bilinear quantum stochastic differential equations (QSDEs). Firstly, real coordinate transformations that preserve commutation and anticommutation relations are characterized, and relative admissibility between different orthonormal Hermitian bases is formulated. Secondly, strongly aligned subspaces are introduced, based on which decoherence-free subsystems (DFSs) are constructed in general orthonormal Hermitian basis as well as the generalized Gell-Mann basis. Thirdly, conditions for the existence of quantum nondemolition (QND) variables are given in terms of both linear systems theory and spectral separation by output-signal observables. Finally, a sufficient condition for quantum back-action-evading (BAE) measurements is established. A four-qubit nearest-neighbor Heisenberg chain with collective dephasing illustrates these structural properties of quantum finite-level systems.
tldr: The paper structurally analyzes finite-level quantum systems in the Heisenberg picture using bilinear quantum stochastic differential equations, characterizing decoherence-free subsystems, quantum nondemolition variables, and back-action-evading measurement conditions.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a comprehensive system-theoretic structural analysis of finite-dimensional quantum systems, focusing on observable evolution and measurement-compatible subspaces rather than state-based dynamics.
method: They characterize real coordinate transformations preserving commutation/anticommutation relations, introduce strongly aligned subspaces to construct decoherence-free subsystems in general Hermitian and generalized Gell-Mann bases, and derive conditions for QND variables and BAE measurements.
result: Conditions for DFS construction, QND variable existence, and a sufficient condition for BAE measurements are established, illustrated with a four-qubit nearest-neighbor Heisenberg chain under collective dephasing.
conclusion: The work offers a unified Heisenberg-picture framework for structural properties of finite-level quantum systems relevant to decoherence avoidance and measurement back-action evasion.

title: Resonant-pair Energy Return Beyond The Early Green-Kubo Plateau In A Quartic Chain
authors: Julian Olszewski, Zijian Liu, Jie Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distinguishing rapid local energy exchange from sustained transport matters when thermal conductivity is inferred from finite simulations. In a weakly coupled chain of separable quartic oscillators, we identify a quantitative mechanism that changes an early Green--Kubo plateau: resonant neighbors exchange energy and coherently return it. The pair heat-current integral maps to the classical pendulum trapping response. Quartic homogeneity gives an energy-independent reference period [MATH], where [MATH] is the coupling. Without fitted parameters, the leading response predicts a negative first minimum at [MATH] with depth [MATH] times the independent-cell exchange coefficient. Isolated-pair simulations test this reference and resolve finite-coupling corrections. The chain reaches its first minimum on the same time scale, with a shallower minimum and a small later residual. Comparisons with chaotic cells and energy-conserving noise show regimes in which coherent return is absent or interrupted over the measured windows. These finite-time results provide a quantitative reference for separating the early exchange plateau from subsequent correlated dynamics.
tldr: The paper identifies a resonant-pair energy-return mechanism that alters the early Green-Kubo plateau in a classical weakly coupled quartic oscillator chain.
motivation: Finite-time simulations are often used to infer thermal conductivity, so distinguishing transient local energy exchange from sustained transport is important for interpreting Green-Kubo plateaus.
method: The authors analyze a chain of separable quartic oscillators, derive an energy-independent reference period from quartic homogeneity, and compare predictions with isolated-pair and full-chain simulations, including chaotic-cell and noise comparisons.
result: Resonant neighboring oscillators coherently exchange and return energy, producing a negative first minimum in the pair heat-current integral whose depth and timing are predicted without fitting parameters.
conclusion: The work provides a quantitative finite-time reference for separating early exchange plateaus from later correlated dynamics in thermal transport simulations.

title: Time-reversal-based Quantum Metrology In A Central-spin Architecture: From Satin To Butterfly Echo
authors: Sayan Choudhury Aditya Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate quantum-enhanced time-reversal-based metrology using the central spin model, in which a single ancilla spin of magnitude [MATH] mediates interactions between [MATH] bath spins through a star-graph topology. Furthermore, we establish that this platform provides a pathway to perform the butterfly echo protocol by conjugating each evolution step with a random collective bath rotation, thereby achieving axis-agnostic Heisenberg-scaled sensing. Crucially, with a small [MATH]independent number of random steps, the butterfly echo reaches a Fisher information of [MATH] ([MATH] below the Heisenberg limit) for any unknown encoding axis, with the plateau gain tracking the Haar limit. Finally, we demonstrate that the central-spin magnitude [MATH] provides a powerful knob to reduce the optimal protocol timescale without altering the metrological ceiling or the circuit depth required to reach isotropy. motivation: Time-reversal interferometry can boost sensing precision, but achieving axis-agnostic, Heisenberg-scaled sensitivity in a concrete, experimentally accessible platform remains challenging; the central-spin model offers a natural knob (the ancilla magnitude J) to control protocol timescales.
method: Using a central spin of magnitude J mediating all-to-all interactions among N bath spins, the authors analyze the SATIN echo and construct a butterfly echo by conjugating each evolution step with random collective bath rotations, computing the resulting quantum Fisher information with collective readout.

title: Classification Of Binary, Ternary And Quaternary Hermitian Lcd Codes
authors: Keita Ishizuka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend the complete classifications of linear complementary dual (LCD) codes from length 15 to length 19 in the binary case, from length 10 to length 15 in the ternary case and from length 12 to length 13 in the quaternary Hermitian case. The classification rests on a reduction of the monomial equivalence of LCD codes to graph isomorphism on the coordinates, combined with canonical augmentation.
tldr: This paper extends complete classifications of binary, ternary, and quaternary Hermitian linear complementary dual (LCD) codes to larger lengths using a graph-isomorphism reduction with canonical augmentation.
motivation: LCD codes have attracted interest partly because they yield good quantum codes and self-orthogonal-like structures, but exhaustive classification is only known for small lengths; the author aims to push these classification boundaries further.
method: Monomial equivalence of LCD codes is reduced to graph isomorphism on coordinate positions, and canonical augmentation is applied to enumerate all equivalence classes exhaustively.
result: Complete classifications are obtained up to length 19 (binary), length 15 (ternary), and length 13 (quaternary Hermitian), extending previous bounds of 15, 10, and 12 respectively.
conclusion: The work provides enumerated catalogues of LCD codes that may serve as reference tables, though it is a classical coding-theory classification with no direct information-theoretic or quantum-protocol contribution.

title: An Integer Determinant Approach To The Length Of Type Ii Codes And The Weights Of Shadows
authors: Jon-Lark Kim Jae-Hyun Baek
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30809v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well known that the length [MATH] of a binary Type II code is divisible by [MATH]. The classical proof relies on Gleason's theorem on weight enumerators. Motivated by a question of Vera Pless, we give elementary proofs of this fact that avoid invariant theory. Our main tool is a congruence modulo [MATH] for the determinant of the integer Gram matrix [MATH] of a binary orthogonal matrix [MATH], obtained directly from the Leibniz expansion. It gives a short proof of a theorem of Janusz: the number of rows of weight congruent to [MATH] in a binary orthogonal matrix is divisible by [MATH]. From this single statement we derive both the length restriction for Type II codes and the theorem of Conway and Sloane that every vector in the shadow of a binary self-dual code of length [MATH] has weight congruent to [MATH]. We also give two short character-theoretic proofs of the length restriction and explain how all of these arguments detect the Arf invariant of a quadratic form.

motivation: Motivated by a question of Vera Pless, the authors seek proofs of the divisibility of binary Type II code lengths and shadow weight congruences that avoid invariant theory and Gleason's theorem.
method: The main tool is a congruence modulo 4 for the determinant of the integer Gram matrix of a binary orthogonal matrix, derived from the Leibniz expansion; this yields Janusz's theorem on row weights and implies the length and shadow-weight results.

title: On The Role Of Problem Structure In Single-Layer Qaoa
authors: Guilherme Adamatti Bridi, Franklin de Lima Marquezino, Andris Ambainis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Problem structure is regarded as a key factor influencing the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), yet it remains an informal notion without a precise mathematical characterization. In this work, we address this issue by identifying a mathematical object that captures problem structure as seen from the perspective of the target state amplitude in single-layer QAOA. Specifically, we show that this structure is encoded in a joint probability distribution induced by the unique coarsest partition of the computational basis, determined by problem cost values and mixer-dependent walk counts. The statistical dependence between these classes provides a means of quantifying the available problem structure and identifying necessary conditions for exponential amplification. To assess the extent to which this structure can translate into algorithmic performance, we establish a mean-max non-separation bound relating the parameter-averaged probability of measuring the target configuration to its variational maximum. For NPO-PB problems with polynomially many distinct mixer eigenvalues, these probabilities exhibit the same scaling up to polynomial factors. This allows us to characterize the exponential scaling of optimal amplitude amplification by analyzing the parameter-averaged probability without explicitly optimizing the variational parameters. We then derive an exact expression for the parameter-averaged probability as a matrix inner product involving two objects that separately encode the joint structural distribution and the mixer dynamics. This representation provides a framework for identifying the structural mechanisms governing the amplification of the target-state probability or its exponential suppression relative to the mixer capacity. We demonstrate these mechanisms through analytically tractable examples involving transverse field and Grover mixers.
tldr: The paper gives a mathematical characterization of 'problem structure' for single-layer QAOA by encoding it in a joint probability distribution over a coarsest partition of the computational basis, and uses a mean-max non-separation bound to relate parameter-averaged target probabilities to their variational optimum.
motivation: Problem structure is widely invoked to explain QAOA performance but lacks a precise mathematical definition, so the authors aim to formalize it and connect it to conditions for exponential amplitude amplification.
method: They define structure via the coarsest partition of basis states induced by cost values and mixer-dependent walk counts, quantify statistical dependence between classes, prove a mean-max non-separation bound, and derive an exact matrix-inner-product expression for the parameter-averaged target probability.
result: For NPO-PB problems with polynomially many distinct mixer eigenvalues, parameter-averaged and variationally optimal target probabilities scale identically up to polynomial factors, allowing amplification analysis without explicit parameter optimization; mechanisms are illustrated with transverse-field and Grover mixers.
conclusion: The framework identifies structural mechanisms governing amplification or exponential suppression of target-state probability in single-layer QAOA, offering a lens for predicting when problem structure yields algorithmic advantage.

title: Structural Cryptanalysis Of Classic McEliece: Assessment Of Claims, Costs And Evidence
authors: Ramses Fernandez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the last two years, classical structural attacks on McEliece with binary Goppa codes progressed further, at the parameters of Classic McEliece, than in the previous four decades: a subexponential and then a quasi-polynomial distinguisher, key recoveries for public challenges with brute-force labels up to [MATH], and conditional key-recovery estimates of about [MATH] to [MATH] per run of a large sparse linear-algebra computation, depending on the parameter set and on whether and how memory access is charged. On September 2026 the German BSI advised against new deployments of the scheme. This paper gives a version-aware critical assessment of these results. It separates proved distinguishers, conditional cost estimates and actual recoveries; analyses in detail Saarinen's HOVER algorithm, his conditional cost analysis and his recovery of the TII-254 challenge, together with Weis's cost study of Holdout/Hermite key recovery; and compares the other key-recovery routes and the objections raised against them. Our own analysis finds that the cost model is now the main quantitative uncertainty, with about thirty bits between the cheapest and the most expensive model for the same computation; that for the four larger parameter sets every model considered leaves the conditional estimates far below the targeted levels, whereas for mceliece348864 the shortfall is of the order of the spread between models; that the structural estimates are lower than Grover-accelerated information-set decoding for the four larger sets in essentially every model and comparable for mceliece348864; and that none of this is a demonstrated attack, since the underlying heuristics have been tested only on instances tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of times smaller than the target. We close with open questions.
tldr: A critical, version-aware assessment of recent structural (distinguisher and key-recovery) cryptanalysis of Classic McEliece with binary Goppa codes, arguing that cost-model ambiguity dominates the quantitative claims and that no demonstrated attack exists.
motivation: Recent subexponential and quasi-polynomial distinguishers plus conditional key-recovery estimates against Classic McEliece parameters prompted the German BSI in September 2026 to advise against new deployments, so a careful appraisal of what is proved versus estimated versus actually recovered is needed.
method: The authors separate proved distinguishers, conditional cost estimates, and actual challenge recoveries; they analyze Saarinen's HOVER algorithm and TII-254 recovery and Weis's Holdout/Hermite cost study, compare alternative key-recovery routes and the objections to them, and quantify spread across cost models (including memory-access charging).
result: About thirty bits separate the cheapest and most expensive cost models for the same computation; for the four larger parameter sets all models leave conditional estimates far below target security levels, while for mceliece348864 the shortfall is comparable to the model spread; structural estimates beat Grover-accelerated information-set decoding for the larger sets and are comparable for mceliece348864.
conclusion: The cost model is now the dominant quantitative uncertainty and none of the results constitutes a demonstrated attack, since underlying heuristics are validated only on instances orders of magnitude smaller than target parameters; open questions are listed.

title: Rank Ceiling For Twiddle-Perturbation Faults On The Forward Ntt
authors: Chakshu Gupta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: NIST standardised ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024 for post-quantum key establishment and digital signatures. Both compute forward number-theoretic transforms (NTTs) on secret polynomials. Published attacks zero every fixed multiplier, or twiddle, during Kyber key generation with a single fault, or individual twiddles in one Dilithium signing variant; countermeasures detect or mask these faults. Nonzero replacements preserve invertibility, but the uncompressed correct-minus-faulted transform difference can still expose input information. This paper characterises the linear map from a secret polynomial to this difference under arbitrary static twiddle replacements, including bit-flips. For one fault, rank equals the number of butterflies sharing its twiddle, halving by layer from 128 to 2 for ML-KEM and to 1 for ML-DSA. Known positions, replacement values and the difference determine that many independent linear combinations of input coefficients. With one fault per layer, all but the constant and linear coefficients for ML-KEM, or the constant for ML-DSA, are determined; Lean 4 certifies this rank-and-kernel result. Those coefficients cancel for every fault set and choice of replacement values. NIST permits seed storage, motivating comparison of a known correct key with a released faulty key from the same seed. If only one ML-KEM secret-polynomial NTT is faulted, the key difference is a known matrix column times the transform difference; an invertible column entry reconstructs the latter. For ML-DSA, neither reconstruction nor the number of secret-polynomial candidates from compressed key differences is established. The per-layer ranks give a closed-form measure of raw exposure for countermeasure design.
tldr: The paper characterizes the linear map from a secret polynomial to the difference between correct and twiddle-faulted forward NTTs in ML-KEM and ML-DSA, deriving per-layer ranks and kernel structure that quantify raw secret exposure.
motivation: NIST-standardized ML-KEM and ML-DSA compute forward NTTs on secret polynomials, and single-fault twiddle perturbations—even when invertible—can leak input information through the uncompressed transform difference, motivating a precise exposure measure for countermeasure design.
method: For arbitrary static twiddle replacements (including bit flips), the authors analyze the linear map to the correct-minus-faulted difference, showing rank equals the number of butterflies sharing the faulted twiddle (halving per layer from 128 down to 2 for ML-KEM and 1 for ML-DSA), with a Lean 4-certified rank-and-kernel result and an analysis of known-correct-versus-released-faulty-key comparisons under seed storage.
result: One fault per layer determines all ML-KEM coefficients except the constant and linear ones (only the constant for ML-DSA), and these residual coefficients cancel for every fault set and replacement choice; for ML-KEM a single faulted secret-polynomial NTT allows reconstruction of the transform difference via an invertible matrix column entry, while for ML-DSA neither reconstruction nor candidate counting is established.
conclusion: Per-layer ranks provide a closed-form measure of raw secret exposure from twiddle-perturbation faults, offering guidance for fault-countermeasure design in post-quantum KEM and signature implementations.

title: Chordal Construction Of Column-Twisted Reed--Solomon Codes
authors: Krishna Kaipa Anuj Kumar Bhagat
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A [MATH] Generalized Reed--Solomon (GRS) code can be represented, up to monomial equivalence, by a projective system consisting of [MATH] points on a degree [MATH] rational normal curve (RNC) [MATH] in PG[MATH]. We use the term codes broadly for [MATH] codes whose projective system contains at least [MATH] points on a [MATH] of PG[MATH]. By a chord of [MATH], we mean a line which is either a tangent, a real secant, or an imaginary secant of [MATH]. Roth and Lempel constructed non-GRS MDS [MATH] codes by considering projective systems consisting of [MATH] points on [MATH] together with a point on a tangent line. More recently, Liu et al. obtained non-GRS [MATH] MDS codes by considering projective systems consisting of [MATH] points on [MATH] together with a pair of points on a real secant. In the case when [MATH] is odd, the length of these codes satisfies [MATH]. In this article, we construct non-GRS [MATH] MDS codes by considering projective systems consisting of [MATH] points on [MATH] together with a pair of Galois conjugate points on an imaginary secant. For odd [MATH], these codes have lengths satisfying [MATH], thereby improving both the attainable lengths and dimension ranges of previous TRS and CTRS constructions. In particular, our code attains the length [MATH] for every [MATH]. We use a geometric argument to establish the non-GRS property of CTRS codes for the range [MATH], while the traditional method of comparison with the Schur square of GRS codes proves the non-GRS property only for the narrower range [MATH]. We also determine the structure of the dual of any CTRS code.
tldr: The paper constructs new non-GRS MDS codes of column-twisted Reed–Solomon type by placing pairs of Galois-conjugate points on imaginary secants of a rational normal curve, extending attainable length and dimension ranges.
motivation: Generalized Reed–Solomon codes are the canonical MDS codes, and producing non-GRS MDS codes with larger lengths and dimensions is a long-standing combinatorial/algebraic coding problem; previous tangent-line and real-secant constructions impose restrictive length bounds for odd q.
method: Projective-system (arc) geometry in PG(k-1,q): a degree-k rational normal curve plus a pair of Galois-conjugate points on an imaginary secant defines a column-twisted RS code; non-GRS is shown via a geometric argument for a wider parameter range than the Schur-square comparison method, and the dual structure is derived.
result: The construction yields non-GRS [n,k] MDS codes over odd q with improved length and dimension ranges relative to prior TRS/CTRS constructions, achieving a specific length for every admissible k, and the duals of all CTRS codes are characterized.
conclusion: Imaginary-secant projective systems give a strictly larger family of non-GRS MDS codes than tangent/real-secant approaches, and the geometric non-GRS proof outperforms the Schur-square technique.

title: Lean-QuantumAlg: A Framework For Ai Agents To Produce Quantum Algorithms That Humans Can Trust
authors: Lei Zhang, Mingrui Jing, Yusheng Zhao, Jiahong Liu, Xin Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of constructing quantum algorithms and proofs, yet machine-checked proofs alone cannot guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims match the verified computation.Here we introduce Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for trustworthy AI-assisted development of quantum algorithms.Its Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract binds correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration and quantum and classical resource bounds to a single execution, while separating the guarantees that Lean checks from the problem specifications and execution models that humans review. We demonstrate the framework on nine AI-formalized quantum algorithms, from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256, with less than 1% of each algorithm's imported source code requiring statement-level human review once the shared framework has been audited. By integrating reusable mathematical foundations, certified algorithmic primitives and execution-grounded verification, Lean-QuantumAlg provides a basis for AI agents to construct and certify quantum algorithms, opening a path toward scalable AI-driven discovery of quantum algorithms.
tldr: Introduces Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for AI agents to formally verify quantum algorithms with explicit correctness, success-probability, state-restoration, and resource-bound contracts.
motivation: AI-generated quantum algorithms and machine-checked proofs do not by themselves guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims are accurate.
method: The framework defines an Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract tying correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration, and quantum/classical resource bounds to a single execution, separating Lean-checked guarantees from human-reviewed specifications and execution models.
result: The authors demonstrate the framework on nine AI-formalized algorithms, from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256, with under 1% of imported source code requiring statement-level human review after the shared framework is audited.
conclusion: Lean-QuantumAlg provides a basis for scalable, trustworthy AI-driven discovery and certification of quantum algorithms, though it sits outside the researcher's core information-theoretic, thermodynamic, networking, or hybrid-systems interests.

title: Photon Localization: Local Measurements, Localized States, And Causality
authors: Johannes Skaar Jan Gulla
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We review what it means for a relativistic particle to be localized and argue that the most useful approach is through local measurement. This perspective ties localization directly to relativistic causality and measurable outcomes in spacetime. Strict localization in quantum field theory is formalized by states that give the same expectation value as vacuum for all local observables outside some spacetime region. With this formalism, single photons cannot be strictly localized, but coherent states can. The structure and interpretation of local observables and local operator algebras are discussed in connection with the Reeh-Schlieder theorem. Since probabilities of local measurement outcomes cannot vanish in vacuum, particle detection events must be phrased carefully. Key characteristics of strictly localized states are surveyed alongside concrete strategies for constructing them. The relationship between localization, causality, and on-demand sources is analyzed, finding that strictly localized states can represent localized, propagating information in quantum field theory. Explicit examples of localized photonic states are presented with an emphasis on quantum optics, including states that approximate single photons and (entangled) Bell states.
tldr: The paper reviews photon localization through local measurements and quantum field theory, arguing that strict localization is tied to relativistic causality and can be formulated using states indistinguishable from vacuum outside a spacetime region.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify what it means for a relativistic particle, especially a photon, to be localized and to connect localization to causality and measurable outcomes in spacetime.
method: Strict localization is formalized via states that match vacuum expectation values for all local observables outside a spacetime region; local observables and operator algebras are discussed in connection with the Reeh-Schlieder theorem, and construction strategies for localized states are surveyed.
result: Single photons cannot be strictly localized, whereas coherent states can; local measurement outcome probabilities cannot vanish in vacuum, so detection events must be phrased carefully; explicit localized photonic states approximating single photons and entangled Bell states are presented.
conclusion: Strictly localized states can represent localized propagating quantum information in quantum field theory, with implications for on-demand sources and a operational understanding of localization via local measurements and causality.

title: Stochastic Diversity Stabilization In Nonlinear Competitive Dynamics: A Statistical Mechanics Approach To Fluctuation Suppression And Finite-Size Scaling
authors: Ruocun Ou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic forcing can prevent diversity collapse in competitive dynamical systems, yet the quantitative conditions and the dynamical mechanism responsible remain poorly characterized. We address both questions in a class of nonlinear stochastic replicator dynamics on the N-dimensional probability simplex, parameterized by a nonlinearity exponent gamma and additive Gaussian noise of intensity sigma. Under the baseline interaction, the minimum noise required to sustain diversity decays as a power law, sigma_c ~ N^(-alpha); replacing the baseline interaction with a superlinear variant shifts alpha from about 1.1 to about 2.0, in agreement with a linear-stability prediction alpha = (gamma+2)/2, identifying alpha as a model-specific quantity rather than a universal index. Scanning the (gamma, sigma) plane reveals a smooth dynamical crossover: the fluctuation susceptibility chi_H = N Var(H) peaks at gamma ~ 0.7 (chi_H ~ 0.6) and is suppressed at high gamma, with no divergence near gamma ~ 1.4; matched finite-size analysis finds no systematic divergence of the peak with N, ruling out a genuine second-order phase transition. The entropy relaxation time tau_relax(gamma) remains approximately constant (about 2.9 time units) across the full range of gamma, even as chi_H decreases sixfold; this decoupling between relaxation timescale and fluctuation amplitude implies that suppression arises from convergence of diverse pathways to similar endpoints rather than from accelerated relaxation along a single channel. These findings identify nonlinear fluctuation suppression via pathway multiplicity -- distinct from both noise-induced transitions and equilibrium criticality -- as the operative stabilization pattern in this class of nonequilibrium stochastic systems.
tldr: The paper analyzes stochastic replicator dynamics on a probability simplex to explain how additive noise stabilizes diversity and how fluctuation suppression depends on nonlinearity and system size.
motivation: Stochastic forcing is known to prevent diversity collapse in competitive dynamics, but the quantitative conditions and dynamical mechanism are not well characterized.
method: The authors study nonlinear stochastic replicator dynamics with a nonlinearity exponent gamma and Gaussian noise intensity sigma, using stability analysis, finite-size scaling, and numerical scans of fluctuation susceptibility and entropy relaxation time.
result: The critical noise decays as a power law sigma_c ~ N^(-alpha), with alpha depending on the nonlinear interaction; fluctuation susceptibility peaks near gamma ~ 0.7 but shows no finite-size divergence, and relaxation time remains approximately constant while fluctuation amplitude drops.
conclusion: Diversity stabilization arises from pathway multiplicity and convergence of diverse trajectories rather than a genuine phase transition or accelerated relaxation, distinguishing this mechanism from noise-induced transitions and equilibrium criticality.

title: Einstein's Theory Of Brownian Motion: The non-Fickian Normal Diffusion
authors: A. Bhattacharyay
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Einstein's theory of diffusion defines what is considered {\it normal diffusion}. Historically, Einstein considered homogeneous diffusion characterised by a diffusion constant in his original calculations, resulting in what is known as {\it Fickian} diffusion, which thermally relaxes concentration inhomogeneities. However, in the same derivation of Einstein, the seed of generalisation of the theory to {\it non-Fickian} diffusion in the presence of space-dependent diffusivity is hidden. This indicates that non-Fickian diffusion, which can drive concentration inhomogeneities, can also be normal diffusion. The present article discusses the origin of the {\it normal} non-Fickian diffusion in Einstein's theory of diffusion.
tldr: The paper revisits Einstein's theory of Brownian motion to show that non-Fickian diffusion with space-dependent diffusivity can still be normal diffusion.
motivation: The standard classification equates normal diffusion with Fickian homogeneous diffusion, but the author argues that Einstein's original derivation contains the seed for a broader non-Fickian normal diffusion regime.
method: The paper provides an analytical discussion and generalization of Einstein's diffusion derivation, focusing on the role of space-dependent diffusivity.
result: It identifies that non-Fickian diffusion, which can drive concentration inhomogeneities, can also be normal diffusion within Einstein's framework.
conclusion: Normal diffusion is not restricted to Fickian diffusion; space-dependent diffusivity yields a normal non-Fickian diffusion class.

title: Scalable Neural Wave Functions Via Information Mixing And Hierarchical Network Architectures
authors: Stefanie Czischek Faith Oyedemi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerically simulating quantum many-body systems is one of the central challenges in modern physics, as the exponential growth of the Hilbert space with system size renders large-scale exact solutions intractable. Over the past decade, generative artificial neural networks have emerged as powerful wave function ans\"atze that have powered advances in finding ground state representations, reconstructing quantum states from data, and modeling dynamics in quantum many-body systems. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are computationally efficient, the recurrent nature can limit their capacity to capture long-range correlations. Transformer models with their underlying self-attention mechanism excel at capturing these long-range correlations, but incur increased computational requirements, restricting applications to small physical systems. In this work, we address these limitations by exploring the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) mixer model as a wave function ansatz. By mixing information globally and locally through the system via a computationally lightweight mixing strategy, this architecture promises to combine the ability to capture long-range correlations with low computational costs. We benchmark the model on finding ground state representations of two-dimensional quantum many-body systems in various phases of matter and investigate the behavior of representational accuracy and computational efficiency for different physical system sizes. By comparing its performance to RNNs and transformer models with single-site and patched input definitions, we demonstrate that the MLP mixer architecture performs competitively with state-of-the-art network models. We further show that a hierarchical combination of this model with the transformer model outperforms other state-of-the-art architectures for large-scale quantum systems, opening new avenues for investigating quantum phases of matter.
tldr: The paper introduces an MLP-mixer neural wave-function ansatz with hierarchical transformer combinations to scale simulations of quantum many-body ground states.
motivation: Exact simulation of quantum many-body systems is intractable due to Hilbert-space growth, and existing RNN and transformer wave-function ansatze face tradeoffs between long-range correlation capture and computational cost.
method: The authors explore an MLP-mixer architecture that globally and locally mixes information across the system, benchmark it on 2D quantum many-body ground states, and compare against RNNs and transformers with single-site and patched inputs.
result: The MLP mixer performs competitively with state-of-the-art network models, and a hierarchical MLP-mixer/transformer combination outperforms other architectures for large-scale systems.
conclusion: The work suggests lightweight information-mixing architectures can improve scalable neural quantum-state representations, opening avenues for studying quantum phases of matter.

title: Laser With $7\times10^{-18}$ Stability
authors: Ben Lewis, Zoey Z. Hu, Dahyeon Lee, Kyungtae Kim, William Warfield, Kai Zhou, Daniele Nicolodi, Thomas Legero, Uwe Sterr, Fritz Riehle, Jun Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report a laser with record frequency stability, based on a 21 cm cryogenic silicon cavity. For best short-term stability, the cavity operates at 6 K to minimize Brownian thermal noise and achieves a fractional stability of [MATH] between 2 to 50 s of averaging time and 2.5 mHz linewidth. For best long-term stability the cavity operates at 16 K, where silicon has a zero-crossing of thermal expansion. Slightly increased thermal noise limits the performance to [MATH], consistent with the expected temperature scaling, but the long-term performance is improved. The laser then has a linewidth of 2.9 mHz and long-term frequency drift less than 4 {\mu}Hz s[MATH]. The laser is used to enhance the performance of a state-of-the-art Sr lattice clock, operating with Rabi and Ramsey interrogation times beyond 10 s.
tldr: The authors demonstrate a record-stability laser based on a 21 cm cryogenic silicon cavity, reaching fractional frequency stability of ~7×10⁻¹⁸ and millihertz linewidths, and use it to improve a Sr optical lattice clock.
motivation: Ultra-stable lasers are needed to push optical atomic clock performance and to probe fundamental physics; thermal noise and thermal expansion in the reference cavity are the key limits to address.
method: A 21 cm single-crystal silicon cavity is operated at 6 K to suppress Brownian thermal noise for short-term stability and at 16 K, near the zero-crossing of silicon's thermal expansion, for long-term stability; the laser is then applied to a state-of-the-art Sr lattice clock with interrogation times beyond 10 s.
result: The 6 K operation yields ~7×10⁻¹⁸ fractional stability between 2 and 50 s with 2.5 mHz linewidth, while the 16 K operation gives 2.9 mHz linewidth and drift below 4 μHz/s at somewhat reduced thermal-noise-limited stability.
conclusion: Cryogenic silicon cavities provide a route to lasers with stability at the 10⁻¹⁸ level, enabling longer interrogation of optical clocks and improved clock performance.

title: Matrix Triangle Inequalities: Past, Present, And Future
authors: Teng Zhang Jean-Christophe Bourin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30538v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This survey provides a concise overview of matrix triangle inequalities. Classical topics, such as inequalities for unitarily invariant norms, are revisited from a different perspective, with a particular emphasis on unitary orbit inequalities and various notions of matrix moduli. The exposition progresses from elementary results to much more recent developments, highlighting the evolution of the subject and its ongoing directions of research.
tldr: A concise survey of matrix triangle inequalities, focusing on unitarily invariant norms, unitary orbit inequalities, and matrix moduli.
motivation: The authors aim to revisit classical matrix inequality results from a unified perspective and connect them to recent developments.
method: The paper is a survey that progresses from elementary matrix inequalities to modern results on unitary orbits and matrix moduli.
result: It provides an organized overview of known inequalities and highlights how the subject has evolved and where it may be heading.
conclusion: The survey is a useful mathematical reference for matrix analysis but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Bridging Number-Theoretic Primality Testing And Algorithmic Optimization: An Adaptive Cryptographic Framework
authors: Vo Hoai Viet Tran Minh Thanh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The security of modern public-key cryptographic systems, such as RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ECC, depends entirely on the computational intractability of the integer factorization and discrete logarithm problems. For these asymmetric algorithms to operate, a core requirement is that the system must be capable of generating, testing, and simultaneously proving the primality of extraordinarily large numbers. To meet those requirements, this study proposes a comprehensive framework, bridging clas- sical number theory with modern machine learning models and optimization algorithms. Specifically, the paper delineates an adaptive, arbitrary-precision architecture dedicated exclusively to primality testing. Concurrently, the research deeply analyzes the theoretical foundations of testing methods (both deterministic and probabilistic), hardware-level optimization techniques, and the application of quantum-secured entropy sources, while providing rigorous mathematical proofs to guarantee security even when the prime distribution is biased.
tldr: The paper proposes an arbitrary-precision, adaptive framework for generating, testing, and proving primality of large numbers for public-key cryptography, combining classical number theory with machine-learning heuristics, hardware-level optimization, and quantum-derived entropy sources.
motivation: RSA, Diffie-Hellman and ECC all require reliable generation and certification of very large primes, and existing primality-testing pipelines are either too slow at scale or offer insufficient guarantees when prime distributions are biased.
method: The authors describe an adaptive arbitrary-precision architecture that integrates deterministic and probabilistic primality tests, analyzes hardware-level implementation optimizations, and incorporates quantum-secured entropy sources, supported by mathematical proofs of security under biased prime distributions.
result: The framework is presented as a unified architecture with rigorous proofs guaranteeing correctness/security of primality certification even under adversarial or biased prime sampling, alongside discussion of optimization trade-offs.
conclusion: The work argues that bridging classical number theory, algorithmic optimization, and modern entropy sources yields a practical and provably sound primality-testing framework for deployed asymmetric cryptography.

title: Foundry-Fabricated Silicon Nitride Grating Arrays With Uniform Power Distribution At Visible Wavelengths
authors: Amged Alquliah, Xiaoxin Wang, Jifeng Liu, Anthony Rizzo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiplexed optical biosensors are widely deployed to read out many biological targets in parallel. However, their channel count and integration density are limited by the photonic network that delivers light to individual sensing sites. Existing on-chip networks have been largely developed for phased arrays and image projection, where performance is assessed through an aggregate radiation pattern rather than the local intensity at each output. In this Letter, we demonstrate a novel bus-and-tap network architecture for massively parallel multiplexed optical delivery. The network uses cascaded directional couplers with individually designed interaction lengths, allowing for arbitrary, user-defined illumination patterns not possible with conventional binary tree architectures. We experimentally validated our proposed architecture with 46 visible-wavelength grating emitter channels designed for uniform illumination at 40 [MATH]m pitch in a commercial 300-mm silicon nitride foundry process, achieving an emitted-intensity coefficient of variation of 9.3% at 530 nm, and 8.8% under band-integrated illumination from 550 nm to 650 nm. These results provide a route to scalable visible-light delivery for sensing, imaging, neural interfaces, and parallel optical addressing in quantum systems.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a foundry-fabricated silicon nitride bus-and-tap grating emitter array for uniform visible-light delivery in multiplexed optical biosensing.
motivation: Multiplexed optical biosensors need scalable on-chip photonic networks that deliver uniform power to many sensing sites, which is difficult with conventional binary-tree architectures.
method: The authors design cascaded directional couplers with individually tuned interaction lengths to create arbitrary illumination patterns and validate a 46-channel visible-wavelength grating emitter array in a commercial 300-mm silicon nitride process.
result: The fabricated device achieves uniform illumination at 40 µm pitch with emitted-intensity coefficients of variation of 9.3% at 530 nm and 8.8% under band-integrated illumination from 550 to 650 nm.
conclusion: The bus-and-tap architecture provides a scalable route for visible-light delivery in sensing, imaging, neural interfaces, and parallel optical addressing, but it is not a quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum network, or hybrid quantum systems result.

title: A Sharp Gradient-corrected Lieb--Thirring Inequality In One Dimension With Applications To Density Functional Theory
authors: Louis Garrigue Thiago Carvalho Corso
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We first prove a sharp Lieb-Thirring inequality with semi-classical constant and gradient correction in one dimension. In the periodic setting, the corresponding inequality also includes a parity dependent shell-correction term, which appears to be new. Moreover, we also characterize the optimizers of these inequalities. In particular, the optimizing density profiles form a two-dimensional manifold, which we call here the Poincar\'e density manifold. We then apply these results to study the Thomas--Fermi--von Weizs\"acker (TFW) approximation of the kinetic energy in Density Functional Theory. More precisely, we first obtain an explicit and non-asymptotic bound on the global and local error made by the TFW approximation.
