Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from [MATH] to [MATH] when at most [MATH] ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most [MATH]. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.
tldr: The paper proposes a truthful, computationally efficient mechanism for allocating sponsored content in LLM-generated answers by randomly omitting ads to decouple click probabilities from ad order.
motivation: Generative AI assistants are emerging as advertising media, but ad click-through rates depend on the hosting passage and earlier ads can steal clicks from later ones, making truthful mechanism design difficult.
method: The authors introduce click thinning, a randomized ad-omission scheme that makes each ad's overall click probability order-independent, reducing welfare maximization to a tractable matching problem solved with VCG-style payments.
result: The mechanism is truthful in expectation and achieves at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering, with an improved approximation factor for bounded ads and click-through rates that is optimal for order-preserving rules.
conclusion: Truthfulness and computational efficiency can be achieved simultaneously in LLM-native advertising without additional worst-case welfare loss beyond the order-preserving optimum.

title: BelT Block Cipher
authors: Sergey Agievich, Victor Galinskij, Nikolai Mikulich, Yuriy Kharin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: BelT is a block cipher with a 128-bit block size and a 256-bit key, developed in Belarus and adopted as part of the Belarusian national standard STB 34.101.31 for encryption and integrity control. Its specification was issued as a preliminary standard in 2007, becoming a final standard in 2011. BelT employs an eight-round structure combining elements of a Feistel network and the Lai-Massey scheme. This paper presents a complete description of the cipher and explains the principles underlying its design. Software performance and possible optimizations of BelT are discussed in comparison with those of candidates in the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) competition.
tldr: BelT is a 128-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key adopted in the Belarusian national standard STB 34.101.31, combining Feistel and Lai-Massey design elements.
motivation: The paper aims to document the BelT block cipher and explain its design principles, performance, and optimizations relative to AES competition candidates.
method: It presents a complete specification of the eight-round cipher structure and discusses software implementation performance and possible optimizations.
result: The paper provides a detailed description of BelT and comparative performance analysis against AES candidates.
conclusion: BelT is a classical symmetric-key cryptographic standard, with design and implementation considerations relevant to conventional cryptography rather than quantum information science.

title: First-order Differential Constraints For The Nonlinear Wave Equation:wave Fronts, Admissible Nonlinearities And Exact Solutions
authors: Oleg Kaptsov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct exact solutions of the nonlinear wave equation in three space dimensions by the method of linear determining equations: first-order constraint functions are found as solutions of the linear determining equation, the differential constraints obtained by setting them equal to zero are integrated, and the resulting ansatz is substituted into the equation. Lie point symmetries are a special case, and the solutions obtained generically have no symmetry. The determining equations tie the admissible nonlinearity to the geometry of the constraint: arbitrary on characteristic hyperplanes, cubic on light cones, and, for a pair of constraints, exponential on light cones and quintic on the cylindrical fronts of a line source. Among the solutions are smooth bounded sine-Gordon walls and vortex configurations whose shape varies arbitrarily along a front, the fields of point sources moving on arbitrary trajectories for the cubic and Liouville equations, with an exact nonlinear analogue of the Larmor formula for the power radiated in the cubic case, and smooth finite-energy solutions of the cubic equation with any prescribed number of toroidal nodal surfaces.
tldr: The paper constructs exact solutions of the three-dimensional nonlinear wave equation using first-order differential constraints derived from linear determining equations.
motivation: The authors aim to generate exact, generically non-symmetric solutions of the nonlinear wave equation, generalizing Lie point symmetry methods through the method of linear determining equations.
method: First-order constraint functions are obtained as solutions of a linear determining equation, the resulting differential constraints are integrated, and the corresponding ansatz is substituted into the nonlinear wave equation to fix admissible nonlinearities.
result: Admissible nonlinearities are tied to the geometry of the constraint (arbitrary on characteristic hyperplanes, cubic on light cones, exponential/quintic for pairs of constraints), yielding smooth sine-Gordon wall solutions, vortex configurations, fields of moving point sources with a nonlinear Larmor-type radiation formula, and finite-energy toroidal-node solutions.
conclusion: The differential-constraint approach provides a systematic route to exact, symmetry-free solutions of nonlinear wave equations, with rich geometric structure in the admissible nonlinearities.

title: Ergodic Linear-Quadratic Optimal Control With Stochastic Coefficients
authors: Nizar Touzi Xuyang Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate ergodic linear-quadratic optimal control problems with stochastic coefficients and introduce the associated stochastic ergodic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, in which the classical ergodic constant is replaced by a random process [MATH]. We establish well-posedness of the equation and show that [MATH] characterizes the optimal ergodic costs for a general class of averaging kernels, including those corresponding to normalized finite-horizon and discounted costs. For random-periodic coefficients, we construct a random-periodic solution and show that the optimal ergodic costs associated with all admissible averaging kernels coincide. We also establish stability of the optimal ergodic costs under perturbations of the coefficients.
tldr: The paper studies ergodic linear-quadratic optimal control problems with stochastic coefficients and introduces a stochastic ergodic Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation whose ergodic constant is a random process.
motivation: Classical ergodic control theory assumes deterministic coefficients and a single ergodic constant; the authors aim to extend it to randomly varying environments where the long-run average cost itself becomes a random quantity.
method: They formulate the stochastic ergodic HJB equation, prove its well-posedness, and show that the random ergodic constant characterizes optimal ergodic costs for a general class of averaging kernels, including finite-horizon and discounted normalizations; for random-periodic coefficients they construct a random-periodic solution and analyze stability under coefficient perturbations.
result: Well-posedness of the stochastic ergodic HJB equation is established, all admissible averaging kernels yield coincident optimal ergodic costs in the random-periodic case, and the optimal ergodic costs are shown to be stable under perturbations of the coefficients.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous foundation for ergodic LQ control in stochastic environments, extending classical ergodic theory to random-periodic settings and showing robustness of the optimal ergodic cost.

title: Dbdsvdmr3: An MRRR-Based Bidiagonal Svd Solver Built From Dstegr
authors: James Demmel, Inderjit Dhillon, Sai Surya Duvvuri, Julien Langou, Osni Marques, Ryan Schneider
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The optimal algorithm for the symmetric tridiagonal eigenvalue problem is Multiple Relatively Robust Representations (MRRR or MR[MATH]), which is capable of computing [MATH] eigenvalue/eigenvector pairs in only [MATH] floating-point operations. While MRRR is nearly 30 years old, it has never successfully been adapted to the bidiagonal SVD. This is not for lack of trying; two previous attempts produced implementations that were considered for LAPACK but eventually abandoned, a result of the fact that neither was reliable enough when run on test problems. The question therefore remained: is there a problem with the theory of MRRR for the bidiagonal SVD or were there simply bugs in the previous implementations that went undetected? This paper resolves this question by presenting DBDSVDMR3 -- a new implementation of the MRRR-based algorithm for the bidiagonal SVD originally proposed by Willems and Lang [ETNA 2012], which, for the first time, performs well on a variety of test problems while achieving significant speedups over both LAPACK's bisection-based solver and, in certain cases, divide-and-conquer for the bidiagonal SVD (thereby indicating that the theory is sound). DBDSVDMR3 will be available in the next release of LAPACK. In this paper, we discuss the design of our implementation, which was obtained with the help of Claude Code, and exhibit its performance on a diverse set of test problems.
tldr: DBDSVDMR3 is a new, reliable implementation of the MRRR-based bidiagonal SVD algorithm that finally performs well on test problems and will ship in LAPACK.
motivation: MRRR achieves optimal O(n^2) complexity for the symmetric tridiagonal eigenproblem but had never been successfully adapted to the bidiagonal SVD, with two prior attempts abandoned for unreliability, leaving open whether the theory or the implementations were at fault.
method: The authors implement the Willems–Lang MRRR algorithm for the bidiagonal SVD (with assistance from Claude Code), designing numerically robust representations and deflation criteria, and validate performance across a diverse suite of test problems against LAPACK's bisection and divide-and-conquer solvers.
result: DBDSVDMR3 is the first MRRR-based bidiagonal SVD solver to be reliable on standard test problems, achieving significant speedups over bisection-based LAPACK routines and, in some cases, over divide-and-conquer.
conclusion: The results indicate the underlying MRRR theory for the bidiagonal SVD is sound and the earlier failures were implementation bugs; the solver will be included in the next LAPACK release.

title: Continuous-time Analysis And Algorithms For Linear And Convex Quadratic Programs Via Exactly Solvable Differential Inclusions
authors: Gabriel P. Langlois, Akwum Onwunta, J\'er\^ome Darbon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear and convex quadratic programs are fundamental problems in optimization. While many methods have been developed for solving these programs in large-scale applications, to our knowledge none have attempted to solve their continuous-time gradient flow, a differential inclusion, in full generality without assumptions beyond feasibility. Recent work solved the gradient flows in two special cases, basis pursuit and the lasso, and obtained competitive algorithms. Motivated by these results, we solve the general case exactly. Using the minimal selection principle for monotone differential inclusions, we show that the trajectory of the gradient flow consists of finitely many pieces, each obtained from one nonnegative least-squares problem. Its final piece yields an optimal solution or a certificate of unboundedness. This analysis leads to two algorithms. The first algorithm is exact, terminates after finitely many steps, and applies to linear programs and projections onto polyhedra. The second algorithm, which we call minimal selection descent, discretizes the gradient flow for general convex quadratic programs. Its iterates converge to an optimal solution when one exists and otherwise certify unboundedness. We apply both algorithms to a positivity-preserving limiter for a discontinuous Galerkin scheme and to optimal control problems for the Poisson and heat equations. In the limiter, the first algorithm conserves the total mass more accurately than the state-of-the-art Douglas--Rachford splitting method. On the control problems, minimal selection descent reaches the optimal value to machine precision and is competitive in time with commercial and open-source solvers.
tldr: The paper exactly solves the continuous-time gradient flow (a monotone differential inclusion) of general linear and convex quadratic programs via the minimal selection principle, yielding an exact finite algorithm and a descent discretization.
motivation: Prior work solved gradient flows only for special cases like basis pursuit and the lasso; the authors aim to handle the general feasible case without extra assumptions and turn the trajectory analysis into competitive algorithms.
method: Using the minimal selection principle for monotone differential inclusions, the trajectory is decomposed into finitely many pieces, each from a nonnegative least-squares problem; this yields an exact algorithm and a 'minimal selection descent' scheme for convex QPs.
result: The exact algorithm terminates finitely for LPs and polyhedral projections, while minimal selection descent converges to optima or certifies unboundedness; applications to a DG positivity-preserving limiter and Poisson/heat optimal control show machine-precision accuracy and competitive runtime.
conclusion: Continuous-time differential-inclusion analysis provides a unifying, practical route to solving LPs and convex QPs, outperforming Douglas–Rachford splitting in mass conservation for the limiter application.

title: Structure-Preserving Dimension Reduction And Surrogates For Partially Linear Bayesian Inverse Problems
authors: Ziheng Zhang, Dingcheng Luo, Thomas O'leary-Roseberry, Umberto Villa, Omar Ghattas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many Bayesian inverse problems are characterized by two parameter vectors with distinct roles. A medium property, operator coefficient, or geometry block enters the forward model nonlinearly, whereas a volumetric, initial condition, or boundary condition source enters linearly. General-purpose nonlinear surrogates must relearn this known source dependence from data and may not preserve the correct source scaling outside the training regime. We introduce a structure-preserving partially linear (SPPL) framework that constructs separate reduced spaces for outputs, (linearly appearing) sources, and (nonlinearly appearing) medium variables and represents the reduced forward map as an affine function of the retained source coordinates, with coefficients that depend on the medium variables. Here, "affine" refers to the retained, mean-centered source coordinates: the physical forward map remains linear in the source, while the affine offset is induced by the source-prior mean and vanishes when that mean is zero. The analysis first identifies the optimal blockwise ridge approximation and then derives the optimal affine-in-source approximation under independent medium and source priors. A direct decomposition of the forward error into output, source, medium, and surrogate contributions yields blockwise spectral criteria and prior-predictive expected-KL control. For a Gaussian source prior, the optimal affine-in-source approximation coincides with the optimal blockwise ridge approximation. In a coseismic numerical example, a three-model controlled ablation on common block-reduced coordinates separates the effects of coefficient-matrix supervision and structure-preserving affine-in-source parameterization. Reduced-space surrogate MCMC provides orders-of-magnitude online acceleration relative to high-fidelity posterior sampling.
tldr: The paper introduces a structure-preserving partially linear (SPPL) reduced-order surrogate framework for Bayesian inverse problems in which sources enter the forward model linearly while medium properties enter nonlinearly.
motivation: Generic nonlinear surrogates must relearn a known linear source dependence from data and can violate correct source scaling outside the training regime, motivating architectures that build this structure in by construction.
method: Separate reduced spaces are constructed for outputs, linearly appearing sources, and nonlinearly appearing medium variables, with the reduced forward map represented as affine in mean-centered source coordinates and coefficients depending on the medium; optimal blockwise ridge and affine-in-source approximations are derived and errors decomposed into output, source, medium, and surrogate contributions.
result: For Gaussian source priors the optimal affine-in-source approximation coincides with the optimal blockwise ridge approximation, blockwise spectral criteria and prior-predictive expected-KL control follow, and a coseismic ablation shows orders-of-magnitude online speedup for surrogate MCMC.
conclusion: Structure-preserving partial linearity yields accurate, scalable surrogates for MCMC-based Bayesian inversion, though the work lies entirely in computational inverse problems and numerical analysis.

title: Energy-rate Equidistribution For Adaptive Ssav--bdf2 Integration Of Gradient Flows
authors: JF Williams Suki Shergill
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an adaptive time-stepping strategy for scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) schemes combined with variable-step BDF2 discretization for gradient flows. The strategy selects step sizes based on the instantaneous energy dissipation rate and enforces monotonicity of a computable symmetric energy through a step rejection mechanism. We show that the step-size rules used in practice correspond to equidistributing a monitor function along the energy curve, connecting energy-adaptive time stepping to the classical theory of r-adaptive mesh methods. The monitor [MATH] is asymptotically optimal as it minimises the leading-order maximum symmetric-energy discrepancy for a given number of steps. A combined monitor that switches to [MATH] near equilibrium caps step growth without degrading this error bound. The arclength parameter [MATH] used in prior work is shown to be the ratio of the largest permitted step to the energy-error tolerance. The controller is paired with the SSAV--BDF2 discretization. Accepted steps satisfy monotonicity of the symmetric energy, from which we deduce a bound on the physical energy that is uniform in the number of steps, [MATH], and the scheme achieves second-order global accuracy under standard step-ratio restrictions. Numerical experiments on Cahn--Hilliard, Ohta--Kawasaki, Phase--Field Crystal, and functionalized Cahn--Hilliard models confirm the theory and demonstrate the method's efficiency.
tldr: The paper develops an adaptive time-stepping strategy for SSAV-BDF2 discretizations of gradient flows, based on equidistributing the instantaneous energy dissipation rate.
motivation: Adaptive step-size selection for energy-stable schemes for gradient flows is needed to balance accuracy and efficiency while preserving monotonicity of a discrete energy.
method: The authors design monitor functions tied to the energy dissipation rate, prove the step-size rules correspond to r-adaptive mesh equidistribution, derive an asymptotically optimal monitor, and combine it with SSAV-BDF2 discretization with step rejection.
result: Accepted steps guarantee monotonic symmetric energy, giving an energy bound uniform in step number and second-order global accuracy under step-ratio restrictions, confirmed numerically on Cahn-Hilliard, Ohta-Kawasaki, phase-field crystal and functionalized Cahn-Hilliard models.
conclusion: The work links energy-adaptive time stepping to classical r-adaptive mesh theory and yields an efficient, provably stable integrator for gradient-flow PDEs.

title: MPIDetector: Detecting Multi-modal Prompt Injection Via LLM-based Reasoning
authors: Jingyue Li Yiheng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rapid integration of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) into real-world applications, Prompt Injection (PI) has emerged as a critical security threat. Attackers can conceal malicious instructions within textual narratives or visual inputs to bypass safety alignment. Existing approaches, such as signature- and perplexity-based methods, rely heavily on pattern matching, making them insufficient to detect sophisticated, cross-modal PI payloads. In this paper, we propose a novel detection framework, called MPIDetector, that leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities via few-shot In-Context Learning (ICL). Instead of fine-tuning, we provide the model with specific prompt templates and representative attack examples, enabling it to scrutinize the semantic intent of input across modalities. We constructed a comprehensive evaluation benchmark comprising eight textual and seven visual malicious categories, supplemented with benign datasets to rigorously test for false positives. Our evaluation across multiple leading LLMs, including Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash, demonstrates the efficacy and generalizability of this approach. The proposed method achieves up to 90.91% accuracy and 100% recall on textual tasks. In the visual domain, it achieves up to 99.28% accuracy while maintaining 100% precision across all evaluated models. Crucially, when evaluated against 500 highly obfuscated environmental web-agent injections (WebInject), MPIDetector achieved a detection rate up to 99.80%. Comparisons with two baseline approaches for detecting textual PI payloads, along with two additional methods for visual input detection, demonstrate MPIDetector's superior accuracy. These results show that LLM-driven reasoning provides a robust, cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injections.
tldr: MPIDetector is a few-shot in-context-learning framework that uses LLMs' reasoning to detect multi-modal prompt injection attacks in text and images.
motivation: Prompt injection in multi-modal LLMs is a growing security threat, and existing signature- or perplexity-based detectors rely on pattern matching that fails against sophisticated cross-modal adversarial payloads.
method: Rather than fine-tuning, the authors supply handcrafted prompt templates plus representative attack exemplars so an LLM can semantically scrutinize intent across modalities; they also build a benchmark of eight textual and seven visual malicious categories with benign controls.
result: Across Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and Doubao-seed-1.6-flash the method reaches up to 90.91% accuracy / 100% recall on textual tasks and 99.28% accuracy with 100% precision on visual tasks, and up to 99.80% detection on 500 obfuscated WebInject cases, outperforming four baselines.
conclusion: LLM-driven reasoning with in-context examples offers a robust, generalizable cross-modal defense against advanced prompt injection, though the work lies outside quantum information science.

title: Who Patches The Lightning Network? Evidence From Release Lines In Gossip, 2023-2026
authors: Saurabh Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30350v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning payment network disclosed security vulnerabilities in 2026, and every advisory told operators to upgrade. Whether they do has never been measured, because Lightning gossip carries no software version. Matching the feature bits a node announces against the source of every LND, Core Lightning, Eclair and LDK release, we show that gossip reveals a node's release line after all. Where Core Lightning nodes state their version, the inferred line is exact for 132 of 136 node-line pairs. Across 814 daily snapshots of the public graph from 2023 to 2026, the network patches on release and platform schedules, not on disclosures. Half of LND nodes upgrade within 88 days of a release; small nodes and those that skipped releases lag far behind. The three largest upgrade waves came about a day after the Umbrel app store shipped a new LND version. Since June 2025, 17% of LND upgrades came in the 48 hours after a platform release, windows that cover 4.4% of the time. Disclosures, a median 256 days after the fix, moved few operators: of 12 we can test, only Core Lightning's of July 2026 sped up upgrades, and only among nodes one release line behind. Its later call to restart offline was followed mostly by nodes already patched. Two months after Lightning Labs' August 2026 batch, 71% of the LND nodes exposed at disclosure still ran an affected release. For maintainers, the lever on the nodes that lag is the platforms that package their releases.
tldr: By fingerprinting Lightning Network gossip feature bits against release source code, the paper reconstructs node software versions and measures how operators actually respond to security disclosures across 2023-2026.
motivation: Every Lightning implementation disclosed vulnerabilities in 2026, but whether operators patch has never been measured because gossip carries no version field; understanding patching behavior matters for the security of a widely deployed payment network.
method: The authors match announced feature bits to the source of each LND, Core Lightning, Eclair and LDK release to infer release lines, validate this inference against nodes that self-report versions, and then analyze 814 daily snapshots of the public graph.
result: Upgrades track release and platform schedules rather than security disclosures: median 88 days for LND, with the three largest waves following Umbrel app-store releases, and 71% of nodes exposed at disclosure still vulnerable two months later.
conclusion: Platforms that package Lightning releases are the effective lever for patching laggards, so maintainers and researchers should treat distribution channels, not advisories, as the primary intervention point.

title: Beyond End-to-End Recovery: Towards A Better Understanding Of Llm Steganography Via Rolewise Decomposition
authors: Om Tailor, Yucheng Pan, Solaleh Mohammadi, Xinyan Liu, Kaiqing Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.
tldr: The paper introduces a rolewise decomposition framework for LLM steganography that separately evaluates how private messages are encoded in encoder text, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish, going beyond end-to-end recovery metrics.
motivation: End-to-end recovery is the standard metric for LLM steganography but conflates encoding failures with decoding failures and gives no insight into how the hidden message is actually represented in the transmitted text.
method: The authors decompose the steganographic pipeline into encoder-representation, decoder-recovery, and deterministic-verification stages, and analyze 7,200 encoder responses under this framework using word-length and token-initial pattern analysis.
result: They identify 168 verifiable encodings that decoders missed and 706 responses where the private message was recoverable via word-length or token-initial patterns not specified in the encoder's instructions.
conclusion: End-to-end recovery alone obscures important distinctions between encoding and decoding, and separate evaluation is needed to better understand and mitigate the safety risks of LLM steganography.

title: Mig-cow: Transferable Adversarial Attacks On Deepfake Detectors Via Gradient Decomposition
authors: Wonjune Seo, Joonhyuk Baek, Yeseong Jung, Saerom Park
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite recent advances, deepfake detectors remain vulnerable to adversarial examples, particularly in diverse, real-world settings. We propose MIG-COW, a novel adversarial attack framework that generates highly generalizable and visually imperceptible adversarial examples. By combining momentum-integrated gradients with a consensus-orthogonal decomposition, MIG-COW captures both shared and model-specific vulnerabilities across heterogeneous CNN and ViT detectors. On the AADD-2025 Challenge benchmarks, MIG-COW achieves a 99.96% white-box attack success rate (ASR) with high perceptual similarity (SSIM), significantly outperforming existing baselines. However, its limited 7.16% ASR against official black-box targets - despite achieving the best overall score - highlights the ongoing challenge of transferability. We also demonstrate that incorporating low-performing but diverse models in the ensemble can degrade attack effectiveness, underscoring the need for careful surrogate model selection in real-world adversarial settings.
tldr: MIG-COW is an adversarial attack framework that generates transferable, imperceptible perturbations to fool deepfake detectors by combining momentum-integrated gradients with consensus-orthogonal gradient decomposition across CNN and ViT surrogates.
motivation: Deepfake detectors remain vulnerable to adversarial examples, especially when attacks must transfer to unseen, heterogeneous model architectures in real-world black-box settings.
method: The authors decompose gradients from an ensemble of surrogate detectors into shared (consensus) and model-specific (orthogonal) components, integrating momentum to stabilize updates and improve transferability while preserving perceptual similarity.
result: MIG-COW reaches 99.96% white-box attack success rate with high SSIM on AADD-2025 benchmarks, but only 7.16% ASR against official black-box targets; including weak but diverse surrogates can reduce attack effectiveness.
conclusion: The work highlights the persistent transferability gap in black-box adversarial attacks and argues for careful surrogate model selection in practical adversarial evaluations of deepfake detection.

title: SecLog-Bench: A Scalable Benchmark For Cybersecurity Log Reasoning With Scaffolded Evidence
authors: Yifan Wang, Dongliang Xu, Xiaoyong Li, Jing Li, Peter S. Pan, Yue Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for cybersecurity, leading to growing interest in LLM-based automated cybersecurity log analysis. However, current datasets (1) are limited in scale; (2) rely mainly on single-source evidence; and (3) have only binary or multi-class attack labels, without dense annotations of the reasoning process. To address these limitations, SecLog-Bench has three key features. First, we build an extensible simulation platform that covers 29 attack scenarios, supports repeated execution and the integration of new scenarios, and enables scalable generation of cybersecurity logs with attack-stage labels. Second, we use multi-source logs, including audit logs, application logs, and network traffic, to jointly analyze cyber attacks. Third, we annotate each sample with the essential context for cybersecurity log reasoning and a structured step-by-step evidence chain. We evaluate eight mainstream LLMs on this benchmark for post-detection attack-progress reasoning. Results show that, when provided with scaffolded evidence, current LLMs exhibit modest capability in attack-progress reasoning, with the best model achieving only 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1. Their reasoning remains unreliable; i.e., the highest Stage Reasoning F1 (SRF1) score is only 54.87%. Moreover, even correct predictions may be accompanied by flawed reasoning, and reasoning quality is often misaligned with prediction accuracy.
tldr: SecLog-Bench is a scalable cybersecurity log reasoning benchmark for evaluating LLMs with scaffolded evidence chains.
motivation: Existing cybersecurity log datasets are limited in scale, rely on single-source evidence, and lack dense annotations of the reasoning process.
method: The authors build an extensible simulation platform covering 29 attack scenarios, collect multi-source logs, and annotate samples with structured step-by-step evidence chains.
result: Eight mainstream LLMs achieve at most 44.44% accuracy and 45.07% Macro-F1, with low stage-reasoning F1 and frequent misalignment between prediction accuracy and reasoning quality.
conclusion: Current LLMs remain unreliable for attack-progress reasoning in cybersecurity logs, motivating better benchmarks and reasoning methods.

title: Balanced Posted Prices In Stationary Two-Sided Markets
authors: Ilan Reuven Cohen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study an intermediary that buys nonperishing items from arriving sellers and sells them to arriving buyers, subject to limited storage. Sellers and buyers arrive according to independent Poisson processes. The intermediary pays and charges the same fixed item prices, aiming to maximize long-run gains from trade: buyer value minus seller cost. Our benchmark may choose allocations directly, has unlimited storage, and must purchase each unit before allocating it. Its optimal long-run gain rate equals the value of a linear program of average purchase and allocation rates, with or without knowledge of future arrivals. For buyers whose bundle values are maxima of nonnegative additive valuations (XOS), we compute static common prices that guarantee half of this benchmark for arbitrary finite item capacities, even one storage slot per item, regardless of how ties are resolved without using future arrivals. The prices are computable in polynomial time using demand and supporting-value queries. The construction equalizes itemwise lower bounds on buyer and seller contributions to gains from trade, accounting for procurement costs. We call this contribution balance. As a single-item foundation, we also equalize the rates of purchases and sales selected by the price, before checking inventory availability. We call this rate balance. For capacity [MATH], it yields the tight guarantee [MATH]. The two principles parallel proofs of the classical prophet inequality based on half the expected benchmark and on a median threshold, adapting these balancing ideas to recurring two-sided markets with limited inventory.
tldr: The paper designs balanced posted prices for an intermediary in a stationary two-sided market with Poisson arrivals and limited storage, guaranteeing half of an LP-based benchmark for XOS buyer valuations.
motivation: Intermediaries that buy from arriving sellers and resell to arriving buyers face limited storage and unknown future arrivals, so one needs simple static pricing rules with provable long-run welfare guarantees.
method: The authors formulate an unlimited-storage, clairvoyant benchmark as a linear program over average purchase and allocation rates, then construct static common prices computable in polynomial time via demand and supporting-value queries, using 'contribution balance' (itemwise lower bounds on buyer and seller contributions) and 'rate balance' (equalizing purchase and sale rates).
result: The prices guarantee at least half of the benchmark gain rate for arbitrary finite item capacities, including a single storage slot per item and any tie-breaking rule; for capacity one the rate-balance approach yields a tight guarantee paralleling prophet-inequality proofs.
conclusion: Balancing ideas from prophet inequalities adapt to recurring two-sided markets with inventory constraints, giving robust constant-factor guarantees without knowledge of future arrivals.

title: New Criteria For Upper Bounds On The Number Of Limit Cycles In Li\'enard Systems
authors: Chen Cao, Hebai Chen, Yilei Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study upper bounds for isolated periodic orbits of generalized Li\'enard systems on a single potential well. Common-curvature and common-intercept conditions yield uniqueness and hyperbolicity, while a convex--concave condition on the potential-profile slopes gives an upper bound of two. The statements allow finite unequal potential endpoints; appropriate versions also admit degenerate restoring forces and reduced regularity. We prove a uniqueness extension across slope interfaces, a quantitative joint weak-damping criterion, and a compensation criterion controlled by two derivatives. A separate response comparison at neutral cycles, combined with a connected parameter-family argument, gives a coefficient criterion for a two-cycle bound. Applications include classical quartic systems, negative-parameter and positive-parameter Selkov systems, a uniqueness conjecture for arbitrary-degree polynomial systems, and explicit smooth and nonsmooth examples. Existence is proved separately whenever an exact count is asserted. Restrictions to a potential well, a parameter region, or a compact width interval are retained throughout.
tldr: The paper derives new sufficient conditions giving upper bounds on the number of limit cycles (isolated periodic orbits) in generalized Liénard systems restricted to a single potential well.
motivation: Bounding limit cycle counts in planar polynomial vector fields is a longstanding problem in dynamical systems (part of Hilbert's 16th problem), and generalized Liénard equations provide a tractable setting where structural conditions on damping and potential profiles can yield sharp uniqueness and multiplicity results.
method: The authors impose common-curvature and common-intercept conditions to obtain uniqueness and hyperbolicity, and a convex-concave condition on the potential-profile slopes to bound the count by two; they combine a response comparison at neutral cycles with a connected parameter-family argument, and also handle degenerate restoring forces and reduced regularity.
result: They prove a uniqueness extension across slope interfaces, a quantitative joint weak-damping criterion, and a two-derivative compensation criterion, plus a coefficient criterion for a two-cycle bound, with applications to quartic systems, Selkov systems, and smooth and nonsmooth examples.
conclusion: The work provides new, fairly general criteria for limit-cycle upper bounds and uniqueness in Liénard systems, including a conjecture for arbitrary-degree polynomial systems, but it lies entirely within classical nonlinear dynamics and has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: ReDence: A Hybrid Agentic And Decision-Model Framework For Rapid, Evidence-Grounded Detection Of Modern Social Engineering Scams
authors: Jaishnoor Kaur, Josef Hor\'a\v{c}ek, Ian Waskom, Sayak Saha Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Detecting online social engineering (SE) scams often requires examining website workflows, verifying claims against external sources, and connecting evidence across multiple pages. Existing detectors provide limited support for these investigations, leaving analysts to manually gather and validate evidence, which inevitably delays detection and subsequent takedown of these attacks. To address this gap, we present ReDence, an open-source hybrid framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded detection across diverse SE scam categories. ReDence combines two locally hosted models with complementary responsibilities: a fine-tuned multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) that performs investigative planning, evidence interpretation, and reporting, and a specialized Decider (Tev1) that handles binary and multiple-choice tasks, including browser-action selection, evidence assessment, and decisions about whether to continue an investigation. By delegating discrete decisions to a specialized model, ReDence reduces reliance on lengthy language-model responses, while preserving the reasoning capabilities required for complex investigations. Our evaluation demonstrates that ReDence achieves 96\% accuracy in detecting scams across twelve SE scam categories, substantially outperforming existing detectors while being at least four times faster than comparable agentic models without compromising investigative depth. ReDence also produces structured, evidence-grounded reports that document investigative actions, supporting and contradictory evidence, and collected artifacts, which allow analysts to independently audit detection decisions and utilize the collected evidence to support subsequent mitigation and takedown efforts.
tldr: ReDence is a hybrid agentic and decision-model framework for rapid, evidence-grounded detection of modern social engineering scams.
motivation: Existing scam detectors offer limited support for investigating website workflows and validating claims across multiple pages, forcing analysts to manually gather evidence and delaying detection and takedown.
method: The framework combines a fine-tuned multimodal agentic Investigator (Qwen3.5-4B) for planning, evidence interpretation, and reporting with a specialized Decider (Tev1) for binary and multiple-choice decisions such as browser-action selection and evidence assessment.
result: ReDence achieves 96% accuracy across twelve social engineering scam categories, substantially outperforming existing detectors and running at least four times faster than comparable agentic models while producing structured, evidence-grounded reports.
conclusion: The work improves the speed, accuracy, and auditability of social engineering scam detection, but it is unrelated to quantum information theory, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Matching Tasks To Agents: Mechanism Design For Multi-Agent Contracts
authors: Matteo Bollini, Matteo Castiglioni, Alberto Marchesi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study task assignment under adverse selection and moral hazard. In the single-task setting, agents privately know their types, which determine their success probabilities and effort costs. Based on the agents' reported types, the principal selects an agent to perform the task and offers a success-contingent payment. Although optimal Bayesian contract design is generally computationally intractable and Myerson's characterization does not directly extend to settings with hidden actions and multidimensional private information, we show that the single-task problem admits a simple Myerson-style characterization. Our key insight is that incentive constraints depend only on the ratio between effort cost and success probability. We characterize an optimal mechanism and show that it can be computed in polynomial time. We also establish a tight [MATH] worst-case bound on the ratio between the optimal profit and the full-information benchmark, where [MATH] is the number of agents and [MATH] is the number of types per agent. We then extend our analysis to multiple tasks, showing that an optimal mechanism may not exist. Nevertheless, for a constant number of agents, we provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the supremum profit.
tldr: The paper gives a Myerson-style characterization and polynomial-time algorithm for optimal multi-agent task assignment contracts under adverse selection and moral hazard, plus approximation results for the multi-task case.
motivation: Optimal Bayesian contract design with hidden actions and multidimensional private information is generally intractable, and Myerson's classical characterization does not directly extend to such settings.
method: The authors show incentive constraints depend only on the ratio of effort cost to success probability, derive an optimal mechanism for the single-task problem, and extend to multiple tasks via a polynomial-time approximation scheme for constant agent counts.
result: The single-task optimum is computable in polynomial time with a tight worst-case profit bound relative to the full-information benchmark; for multiple tasks an optimal mechanism may fail to exist, but a PTAS approximates the supremum profit.
conclusion: Contract-theoretic mechanism design with ratio-based incentive structure admits tractable optimal and approximate solutions, with sharp guarantees relative to full-information benchmarks.

title: The Universal Law Of Academic Capital: A Parameter-Unified Theory Of Academic Integritology
authors: Yiguo Zhang, Ruiguang Wang, Xi Chen, Zhengwen Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Academic capital, comprising research funding ([MATH]), accumulated titles and honours ([MATH]), and administrative power ([MATH]), has undergone a silent global decoupling from verifiable epistemic output since the 1990s. Here we present a parameter-unified theory of Academic Integritology that integrates 64 major parameters into a coherent chassis of twelve fundamental equations (Eqs. 0-11b). The theory introduces two computable metrics: [MATH] (net epistemic indispensability) and [MATH] (the Markov-blanket safety boundary of systemic integrity). The [MATH] fraudulence index, defined as [MATH], quantifies this decoupling. Calibrated against retraction data from 40 jurisdictions and the careers of 12 Nobel-caliber scientists, the theory derives a universal law: when [MATH] falls below [MATH], honest research ceases to be an evolutionarily stable strategy. Three jointly necessary levers, raising [MATH], auditing [MATH], and constraining [MATH], restore [MATH]. Three levers, pulled simultaneously, suffice. The theory transforms academic integrity from a moral aspiration into an engineerable system property.
tldr: The paper proposes a 'parameter-unified theory of Academic Integritology' that models the decoupling of academic capital (funding, honours, administrative power) from verifiable epistemic output using twelve equations and two computable metrics.
motivation: The authors claim that since the 1990s academic capital has become silently decoupled from genuine epistemic production, and they aim to turn academic integrity from a moral aspiration into an engineerable system property.
method: They integrate 64 parameters into twelve fundamental equations, define metrics for net epistemic indispensability and a Markov-blanket integrity boundary, and calibrate a fraudulence index against retraction data from 40 jurisdictions and the careers of 12 Nobel-caliber scientists.
result: They derive a 'universal law' stating that when the fraudulence index falls below a threshold, honest research ceases to be an evolutionarily stable strategy, and identify three jointly necessary levers (raising one metric, auditing another, constraining a third) that restore integrity.
conclusion: The authors conclude that pulling all three levers simultaneously suffices to restore systemic integrity, framing academic integrity as an engineerable property.

title: Stiff Source Terms Inside Ader-dg Method
authors: A. P. Popova I. S. Popov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ADER-DG numerical method with the LST-DG predictor, when used to solve hyperbolic equations with stiff source terms, exhibits properties characteristic of IMEX computational schemes. With increasing stiffness, characterized by the parameter [MATH], the maximum of the Courant number [MATH] of the ADER-DG numerical method increases. In the region of strong stiffness [MATH], a linear increase in the Courant number [MATH] occurs. In the region of small source terms [MATH], the results [MATH] transform into known results for the problem [MATH] without source terms. In the transition region [MATH], a range of insignificant decrease in the Courant number [MATH] is discovered. In the linear case, instability is violated precisely when one of the matrix eigenvalues reaches [MATH], regardless of the phase [MATH] of the numerical solution. A rigorous stability theory of the ADER-DG numerical method for stiff problems for arbitrary degree [MATH] of basis polynomials is constructed. The stability condition is simplified to solving a polynomial equation for the Courant number [MATH]. Highly accurate dependencies of the Courant number [MATH] of the ADER-DG method on the parameter [MATH] are obtained. A rigorous direct proof of the approximation of the ADER-DG method is presented. Approximation orders [MATH] for arbitrary degrees [MATH] are rigorously derived. A set of numerical experiments is carried out to apply the ADER-DG method to solving both a linear advection-reaction equation and the system of Euler equations for a two-component reacting medium. The results obtained in these calculations confirm the theoretical results well.
tldr: The paper develops stability and approximation theory for the ADER-DG numerical method with stiff source terms in hyperbolic equations.
motivation: The authors aim to rigorously characterize the Courant-number stability behavior of ADER-DG schemes when source terms become stiff, a regime relevant to IMEX-like computational methods.
method: They construct a stability theory for the ADER-DG method with an LST-DG predictor for arbitrary polynomial degree, reduce the stability condition to a polynomial equation for the Courant number, and prove approximation orders rigorously.
result: The analysis shows that the maximum Courant number increases with stiffness and grows linearly in the strong-stiffness regime, while numerical experiments on linear advection-reaction and reacting Euler equations confirm the theoretical predictions.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous stability and approximation framework for ADER-DG applied to stiff hyperbolic problems, but it lies entirely outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: On The Formal Definition Of Average Function For Interval Data
authors: Sergio F. Alonso, Susana Montes, Susana Diaz-Vazquez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper addresses the formal definition of average functions for interval data, extending classical aggregation theory beyond precise numerical values to the more general setting of real-valued intervals. Recognizing that interval data nat- urally arise in contexts involving imprecision or uncertainty, we examine how established notions of averages and aggregation functions can be generalized when the underlying domain is no longer restricted to the unit interval, but instead encompasses the entire real line. We analyze the impact of different admissible orders on intervals, particularly focusing on the lattice order and several total orders, and provide rigorous definitions of idempotency and mono- tonicity in this context. Furthermore, we adapt and study classical families of aggregation operators such as power means, minimum, maximum, and median to the interval setting, characterizing when these operators satisfy the properties required of average functions for intervals. Our results highlight that the choice of order plays a crucial role in the behavior and suitability of these operators. This work lays a foundation for the systematic aggregation of interval-valued information, with potential applications in statistics, decision making, and fields where data imprecision is inherent.
tldr: The paper formalizes average and aggregation functions for interval-valued data defined over the real line, characterizing how classical operators such as power means, min, max, and median behave under different admissible interval orders.
motivation: Interval data arise naturally in settings with imprecision or uncertainty, yet classical aggregation theory assumes precise numerical inputs, so a rigorous generalization of averaging and aggregation notions to the interval domain is needed.
method: The authors generalize aggregation functions from the unit interval to the full real line, analyze lattice and several total admissible orders on intervals, define idempotency and monotonicity accordingly, and adapt classical operator families including power means, minimum, maximum, and median.
result: They characterize when these interval-valued operators satisfy the properties required of average functions, showing that the choice of admissible order critically determines their behavior and suitability.
conclusion: The work lays a foundation for systematic aggregation of interval-valued information, with potential applications in statistics, decision making, and other areas where data imprecision is inherent.

title: A General Variable Neighborhood Search For Logistic Network Flow Design With Nonlinear Edge Costs And Transshipment Capacities
authors: Alexander Ponomarenko Varvara Kovaleva
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of routing multiple commodities through a logistic transport network so as to minimise the joint cost of vehicle movements and of transshipment (reload) operations at intermediate storages. The problem combines two features that are common in practice but rarely treated together: edge costs that are nonlinear in the transported volume, because freight is carried by vehicles of fixed capacity, and hard upper bounds on the volume that can be reloaded at each node. We formulate the problem as a mixed integer linear program in both an arc-based and a path-based form, derive its linear relaxation, and propose a metaheuristic solver based on General Variable Neighborhood Search (GVNS). The method works in the path space and relies on three problem-specific neighborhoods that generate new candidate paths by (i) shortest paths under a reload-aware metric, (ii) edges carrying partially loaded vehicles, and (iii) detours around congested storages. We evaluate the method on our open benchmark for this problem (arXiv:2606.20653): a corpus of realistic logistic networks calibrated on real road graphs of nine European countries, five U.S. states and the European part of Russia, with near-planar topology (Zipf city sizes, a spatial-network budget model, and a doubly constrained gravity demand model). On 35 synthetic and 15 real-geometry instances with up to 150 storages, GVNS returns solutions within about one percent of the best dual bound on small networks -- a branch-and-bound lower bound substantially tighter than the LP relaxation -- is stable across random seeds, and for a comparable wall-clock budget is up to 55% better than a time-limited exact solver on the medium instances.
tldr: The paper develops a General Variable Neighborhood Search metaheuristic for multi-commodity logistic network flow design with nonlinear edge costs and transshipment capacity constraints.
motivation: Real freight networks combine volume-dependent (vehicle-capacity-induced) edge costs with hard reload limits at intermediate storages, a combination rarely handled jointly in existing optimization approaches.
method: The problem is cast as a mixed integer linear program in arc-based and path-based forms, its linear relaxation is derived, and a GVNS solver working in path space is proposed with three problem-specific neighborhoods (reload-aware shortest paths, partially loaded vehicle edges, detours around congested storages).
result: On an open benchmark of synthetic and real-geometry networks with up to 150 storages, GVNS comes within about one percent of a branch-and-bound dual bound on small instances, is stable across seeds, and outperforms a time-limited exact solver by up to 55% on medium instances.
conclusion: The GVNS approach offers an effective and robust heuristic for capacitated multi-commodity logistic routing with nonlinear costs, supported by a reusable benchmark.

title: The Last Iterate Of The Projected Stochastic Subgradient Method Pays A Logarithm, Even In Dimension One
authors: Guglielmo Beretta, Tommaso Cesari, Roberto Colomboni
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30143v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the projected stochastic subgradient method with the standard anytime stepsizes [MATH] can suffer expected last-iterate optimization error of order [MATH] already on the real line. Combined with the classical in-expectation upper bound, this establishes the sharp worst-case order of the projected stochastic subgradient method.
tldr: The paper establishes a sharp worst-case convergence rate for the last iterate of the projected stochastic subgradient method with anytime step sizes, showing a logarithmic factor is unavoidable even in one dimension.
motivation: Prior work had an in-expectation upper bound for the method's last-iterate error, but the matching lower bound—particularly on the real line—was missing, leaving the true worst-case order undetermined.
method: The authors construct a lower-bound instance on the real line for the projected stochastic subgradient method with standard anytime step sizes, and combine it with the classical upper bound.
result: They show the expected last-iterate error can be of order log(T)/sqrt(T), matching the known upper bound and thus identifying the sharp worst-case order.
conclusion: The analysis closes the gap between upper and lower bounds, proving the logarithmic factor is intrinsic to the method even in the simplest one-dimensional setting.

title: Do Machine Learning-Guided Proactive Full Capacity Protocols Mitigate Emergency Department Overcrowding? A Simulation-Based Evaluation
authors: Khalid Aram, Orhun Vural, Bunyamin Ozaydin, James Booth, Abdulaziz Ahmed
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: Emergency department (ED) overcrowding threatens care quality, yet Full Capacity Protocols (FCPs) are typically activated only after crowding thresholds have been exceeded. This study evaluated whether machine learning-guided proactive FCP activation improves ED crowding control compared with conventional reactive activation. Materials and Methods: We developed and validated an integrated machine learning and discrete-event simulation framework representing ED patient flow and capacity management. An embedded machine learning model predicted hourly waiting-room crowding six hours ahead and triggered proactive FCP activation. Using empirically calibrated operational parameters from a large US hospital, we compared proactive and reactive deployment strategies over a 365-day simulation horizon with 10 independent replications. Outcomes included ED length of stay, wait time, percentage of time above the crowding threshold, number of FCP activations, and protocol duration. Results: Proactive deployment produced statistically significant reductions in the percentage of time above the crowding threshold and average protocol duration across all threshold settings. It also reduced crowding variability and extreme congestion events, resulting in smoother ED operations. Although proactive deployment generally improved ED length of stay and wait time, these differences were not statistically significant. Conclusion: Embedding machine learning predictions within an operational simulation enables proactive, prediction-guided capacity management before severe congestion develops. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of proactive FCP deployment as a decision-support strategy for improving ED crowding control and provide evidence to support prospective implementation in clinical practice.
tldr: A simulation study showing that machine-learning-guided proactive activation of Full Capacity Protocols reduces time spent above ED crowding thresholds compared with reactive activation.
motivation: Emergency department overcrowding degrades care quality, but Full Capacity Protocols are usually triggered only after crowding thresholds are already exceeded, motivating predictive rather than reactive activation.
method: The authors build an integrated machine-learning plus discrete-event simulation model of ED patient flow, using an ML model that forecasts waiting-room crowding six hours ahead to trigger FCP activation, and compare proactive versus reactive strategies over a 365-day horizon with 10 replications using parameters calibrated to a large US hospital.
result: Proactive deployment significantly reduced the percentage of time above the crowding threshold, average protocol duration, crowding variability, and extreme congestion events, while improvements in length of stay and wait time were not statistically significant.
conclusion: Embedding ML predictions in operational simulation supports proactive, prediction-guided capacity management and provides evidence for prospective clinical implementation.

title: A Tutte-Like Theorem For Injective Flows On Meshes
authors: Noam Aigerman Darsh Kaushik
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work proves a theorem regarding injectivity of continuous flows that are defined via discrete vector fields on triangle meshes. In similar fashion to Tutte's embedding, the theorem shows a connection between harmonicity and injectivity. Specifically, a discrete harmonic function is computed over a spherical mesh, and its [MATH]-rotated gradients are taken as the vector field. We show that this leads to an injective flow over the mesh, i.e., when two points are advected along the vector field, their trajectories are guaranteed to not intersect. The core insight behind this theorem is that the characterization of the Poincar\'e-Hopf indices of discrete harmonic 1-forms is paralleled in the combinatorial rules for injective vector fields. Similarly to Tutte's embedding, the injective vector field can be computed by simply solving a sparse linear system. Furthermore, it is differentiably dependent on the entries of the Laplacian, enabling unconstrained gradient-based optimization of the vector field while preserving injectivity. The advection itself can be computed by a quick and accurate algorithm. We experimentally validate the injectivity of the results, as well as show examples of differentiable optimization, such as computing an injective approximation to a given non-injective vector field, and fitting an injective vector field to satisfy constraints.
tldr: The paper proves a Tutte-like theorem guaranteeing that flows generated by rotated gradients of a discrete harmonic function on a spherical triangle mesh are injective (non-self-intersecting).
motivation: Injective (fold-free) vector fields and mappings are essential in geometry processing, and Tutte's embedding provides a classical link between harmonicity and injectivity for planar meshes; the authors seek an analogous guarantee for continuous flows on meshes.
method: A discrete harmonic function is computed on a spherical mesh, its gradients are rotated by 90 degrees to define a discrete vector field, and the Poincare-Hopf indices of discrete harmonic 1-forms are related to combinatorial rules for injective vector fields, yielding a sparse linear system whose solution depends differentiably on the Laplacian.
result: The theorem guarantees that trajectories of points advected along the constructed field never intersect, and experiments confirm injectivity empirically, including differentiable optimization tasks such as projecting a non-injective field onto an injective one and fitting fields to constraints.
conclusion: The work extends Tutte's harmonicity-implies-injectivity paradigm from embeddings to flows, providing a computationally cheap and differentiable construction useful for geometry processing and optimization.

title: Advance Versus Spot Selling In Queueing Systems: The Effect Of Uncertainty Sources
authors: Dongyuan Zhan Yumeng Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an unobservable M/M/1 queueing model to analyze advance selling and spot selling under uncertainty. Customers are heterogeneous in waiting costs, drawn from a uniform distribution. We disentangle two fundamental sources of uncertainty: customer valuation and service capacity. We derive the respective revenue functions for both advance and spot selling strategies and compare their performance. Our analysis reveals that advance selling is more profitable when customer valuations are uncertain. Conversely, spot selling emerges as the more profitable strategy when uncertainty originates from service capacity. When both sources are present, our numerical experiments suggest that the preferred regime depends on the relative dispersion of the two uncertainties: advance selling tends to be favored when valuation uncertainty is sufficiently pronounced relative to capacity uncertainty, whereas spot selling tends to be favored when capacity uncertainty is more pronounced. These results highlight how the origin and magnitude of uncertainty shape the optimal selling strategy in service queues and offer practical guidance for platforms and service providers deciding between advance and spot selling.
tldr: An unobservable M/M/1 queueing model is used to compare advance selling versus spot selling when customer valuation and service capacity are both uncertain.
motivation: Service platforms must choose between selling capacity in advance or on the spot, and it is unclear how the origin of demand/capacity uncertainty should drive that choice.
method: An M/M/1 queue with heterogeneous, uniformly distributed customer waiting costs is analyzed; revenue functions for advance and spot selling are derived analytically and compared, with numerical experiments for the joint-uncertainty case.
result: Advance selling yields higher revenue when valuation uncertainty dominates, while spot selling wins when capacity uncertainty dominates; the preferred regime depends on the relative dispersion of the two uncertainties.
conclusion: The origin and magnitude of uncertainty determine the optimal selling strategy, providing practical guidance for platforms and service providers.

title: Relaxation And $\Gamma$-Convergence Of Stretch Energy On Surface Homeomorphisms
authors: Shu-Yung Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Area-preserving parameterization of triangular meshes is an essential task in geometry processing, yet an exactly area-preserving simplicial mapping may not exist in general. In this paper, we study area preservation of simplicial mappings in the limit of mesh refinement by establishing the [MATH]-convergence of the discrete stretch energy, a functional that measures their area distortion. We first introduce its limit functional, the relaxed stretch energy on surface homeomorphisms, defined through the pushforward of the area measure, and show that it is the relaxation of the stretch energy of diffeomorphisms with respect to uniform convergence. Then, to compare simplicial mappings with homeomorphisms, we construct a geometric lift that requires no shape-regularity assumption on the image mesh. Finally, we establish the [MATH]-convergence and show that the minimal discrete energies converge to the continuum minimum. Moreover, any homeomorphism arising as a limit of lifted discrete local minimizers in fixed-radius balls is area-preserving.
tldr: The paper establishes Γ-convergence of a discrete stretch energy for simplicial mappings of triangular meshes to a continuum relaxed stretch energy on surface homeomorphisms, showing that limits of discrete local minimizers are area-preserving.
motivation: Exactly area-preserving simplicial mappings of triangular meshes generally do not exist, so area distortion must be understood in the mesh-refinement limit.
method: The authors define a relaxed stretch energy via the pushforward of the area measure, prove it is the relaxation of the diffeomorphism stretch energy under uniform convergence, construct a geometric lift without shape-regularity assumptions, and prove Γ-convergence.
result: The minimal discrete energies converge to the continuum minimum, and any homeomorphism arising as a limit of lifted discrete local minimizers in fixed-radius balls is area-preserving.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous variational framework for area-preserving mesh parameterization, bridging discrete and continuum formulations.

title: Matrix-Free Local Multigrid For $c^1$ Hermite Discretizations On GPUs
authors: Micha{\l} Wichrowski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I present a matrix-free local multigrid method for [MATH] tensor-product Hermite discretizations on adaptively refined Cartesian meshes, using the clamped biharmonic problem as the model problem. Extending a cell-wise primal-dual formulation to Hermite elements, I enforce continuity through a constraint operator that is never formed. At refinement edges, geometric prolongation supplies both the trace and its normal derivative, so the local V-cycle needs no edge operator and no hanging-node machinery. For the cubic element, an even-odd decomposition based on the signed reflection symmetry of the Hermite basis, applied along two axes, splits the element matrix into four dense [MATH] blocks and reaches 85% of peak memory bandwidth. Chebyshev-Jacobi and vertex-patch smoothers both preserve conformity by construction. In three dimensions on one NVIDIA A100 in double precision, conjugate gradients preconditioned by the Chebyshev-Jacobi V-cycle need five or six iterations on uniform meshes and solve at up to 4.23 million cells per second. On locally refined meshes the count rises to at most sixteen, ordered by the fraction of cells on a refinement edge and nearly equal for both smoothers.
tldr: A matrix-free local multigrid solver for C^1 tensor-product Hermite discretizations of the clamped biharmonic problem, optimized for GPU execution.
motivation: High-order C^1 Hermite finite elements on adaptively refined meshes typically require explicit constraint operators and hanging-node handling, which is costly; the authors seek a matrix-free, edge-operator-free multigrid scheme that runs efficiently on modern GPUs.
method: Extends a cell-wise primal-dual formulation to Hermite elements with an unformed constraint operator, uses geometric prolongation at refinement edges to supply trace and normal derivative, and applies an even-odd block decomposition of the element matrix together with Chebyshev-Jacobi and vertex-patch smoothers.
result: On a single NVIDIA A100 in double precision, preconditioned CG converges in five to six iterations on uniform meshes (up to 4.23 million cells per second) and at most sixteen iterations on locally refined meshes, achieving ~85% of peak memory bandwidth.
conclusion: The approach yields a scalable, conformity-preserving multigrid preconditioner for high-order biharmonic problems, eliminating hanging-node machinery while maintaining strong GPU performance.

title: Fefferman--Chang-type Atomic Decompositions For Product Hardy Spaces Associated With Schr\"odinger Operators
authors: Agnieszka Hejna-{\l}y\.zwa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a geometric (Fefferman--Chang-type) atomic characterization of the two-parameter Hardy space associated with a pair of Schr\"odinger operators [MATH] on [MATH], [MATH]. The space is defined by the product conical square function. We assume comparability of neighbouring covering cubes, a local bound on the potentials, and decay of the semigroup mass at large scales. We prove that the Hardy norm is equivalent to a sum of classical local product Hardy norms at scales determined by the adapted coverings. This localization formula yields an atomic decomposition whose atoms satisfy size and partial cancellation conditions, with cancellation required only below the corresponding local scales. Both the atoms and their rectangular components remain supported inside fixed enlargements of the covering rectangles. The proof combines one-parameter Schr\"odinger Hardy space characterizations with standard vector-valued arguments and a localized product atomic decomposition with uniform control of scales and supports. The assumptions cover the model case of reverse H\"older potentials [MATH], [MATH], as well as potentials outside every [MATH] class, [MATH], including half-space indicators and exponential potentials.
tldr: The paper proves a Fefferman--Chang-type atomic decomposition for two-parameter product Hardy spaces defined via product conical square functions associated with pairs of Schrödinger operators.
motivation: Product Hardy spaces for Schrödinger operators lack a geometric atomic characterization analogous to the classical Fefferman--Chang theory, which is needed to handle potentials beyond the reverse Hölder class.
method: The authors combine one-parameter Schrödinger Hardy space characterizations with vector-valued arguments and a localized product atomic decomposition that gives uniform control over scales and supports under comparability of neighbouring cubes, local potential bounds, and semigroup mass decay.
result: The Hardy norm is shown equivalent to a sum of classical local product Hardy norms at scales set by adapted coverings, yielding atoms with size and partial cancellation conditions valid only below local scales and supported in fixed enlargements of covering rectangles.
conclusion: The assumptions cover reverse Hölder potentials as well as potentials outside every L^p class, including half-space indicators and exponential potentials, extending product Hardy space theory to a broad class of Schrödinger operators.

title: An F-Type Normal-Reference Calibration For High-Dimensional Covariance Testing
authors: Pengfei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30497v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An F-type normal-reference calibration is developed for testing equality of two high-dimensional covariance matrices with unknown means. The test statistic is a ratio whose numerator measures the Frobenius covariance discrepancy and whose denominator estimates its null expectation. Their difference is the complete Li-Chen statistic. Under suitable moment and trace conditions, we establish a Gaussian-reference approximation. After standardization, the statistic and its reference share the normal or nonnormal limits determined by a convergent normalized spectrum. The reference is a ratio of independent chi-square-type mixtures. Applying Welch-Satterthwaite matching to its two components gives an ordinary F approximation, with degrees of freedom estimated from independent four-observation blocks. The effect of estimating the population means is controlled by an exact expansion, and local-power and consistency results are established. The ordinary F approximation is asymptotically valid under a diffuse spectrum, whereas a covariance spike can produce a nonvanishing approximation error. Simulation studies examine empirical size and power under normal and nonnormal sampling. Averaging the trace estimates over fixed partitions improves their stability, but does not remove size inflation in the strongly correlated settings.
tldr: The paper develops an F-type normal-reference calibration for testing equality of two high-dimensional covariance matrices with unknown means.
motivation: Existing high-dimensional covariance tests based on the Li-Chen statistic lack a simple, accurate reference distribution, so the authors seek a calibrated approximation that remains valid under nonnormal spectra.
method: A ratio statistic comparing Frobenius covariance discrepancy to its estimated null expectation is standardized and matched to a ratio of independent chi-square-type mixtures; Welch-Satterthwaite matching then yields an ordinary F approximation with degrees of freedom estimated from independent four-observation blocks, with mean-estimation effects handled by an exact expansion.
result: The F approximation is asymptotically valid under a diffuse spectrum, but covariance spikes can produce nonvanishing approximation error; simulations show partition-averaged trace estimates improve stability yet do not eliminate size inflation under strong correlation.
conclusion: The proposed F-type calibration offers a practical reference distribution for high-dimensional covariance testing, with identified regimes of validity and residual size distortions in strongly correlated settings.

title: Self-Evolving Static Analysis Via Llm Pseudo-Labeling
authors: Rui Melo, Andre Duarte, Aditya Oke, Shubham Gandhi, Nachiket Kotalwar, Rui Abreu, Lei Li, Carolyn Rose
abstract: ArXiv:2610.30184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries. The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository. The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair.
tldr: SESAA is an LLM-agent framework that iteratively induces and repairs Joern static-analysis queries for Python security bug detection using only LLM-critic feedback, without ground-truth labels.
motivation: Static analysis misses security bugs whenever detection rules have not yet been written for new frameworks, APIs, and idioms, forcing developers to discover failures manually and hand-encode new rules.
